metadata.title: On a density conjecture about unit fractions

nodes.name: Erdős–Graham colouring conjecture for unit fractions
nodes.statement: Erd\H{o}s and Graham \cite{ErGr1980} conjectured that if the integers are coloured by a finite number of colours then there must be such a set which is monochromatic (aside from the trivial $S=\{1\}$).
assumptions: the integers are coloured by a finite number of colours
conclusions: there must be such a set which is monochromatic (aside from the trivial $S=\{1\}$)
nodes.statement_short: Any finite colouring of the integers has a monochromatic finite set S with sum of 1/n equal to 1.

nodes.name: Croot's theorem (colouring version of the Erdős–Graham conjecture)
nodes.statement: If the integers $\{2,3,\ldots\}$ are coloured in finitely many colours there is a monochromatic set $S$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$.
assumptions: the integers $\{2,3,\ldots\}$ are coloured in finitely many colours
conclusions: there is a monochromatic set $S$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$
nodes.label: th-croot

nodes.name: Erdős–Graham density conjecture for unit fractions
nodes.statement: Colouring statements often have a natural strengthening to a corresponding density statement, which Erd\H{o}s and Graham also conjectured\footnote{This conjecture appears on \cite[p. 36]{ErGr1980} and \cite[p. 298]{Gr2013}, for example, as well as in several unpublished notes and letters of Erd\H{o}s as reproduced in \cite{Gr2013}. This conjecture has also been made by Sun \cite{Su2007}.} in this case: that any set of positive density contains some finite $S$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$.
conclusions: contains some finite $S$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$
nodes.statement_short: Every set of positive density contains a finite S with sum of reciprocals equal to 1.

nodes.name: lower and upper density
nodes.statement: Recall that, for any $A\subset \mathbb{N}$, the lower and upper densities of $A$ are defined to be \[\underline{d}(A) = \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{\abs{A\cap [1,N]}}{N}\quad\textrm{and}\quad\overline{d}(A) = \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{\abs{A\cap [1,N]}}{N}\] respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Lower/upper density: liminf/limsup of |A ∩ [1,N]|/N.

nodes.name: density and positive density
nodes.statement: When these limits are equal, $\underline{d}(A)=\overline{d}(A)=d$, we say that $A$ has density $d$ (and say that $A$ has positive density if $d>0$).

nodes.name: Density theorem for unit fractions (Erdős–Graham density conjecture)
nodes.statement: If $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ has positive upper density (and hence certainly if $A$ has positive density) then there is a finite $S\subset A$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$.
conclusions: there is a finite $S\subset A$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$
nodes.statement_short: Every set of positive upper density contains a finite subset whose reciprocals sum to 1.
nodes.label: th-dens

nodes.name: lower and upper logarithmic density
nodes.statement: For any $A\subset \mathbb{N}$, the lower and upper logarithmic densities of $A$ are defined to be \[\underline{\delta}(A) = \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{\log N}\sum_{n\in A\cap [1,N]}\frac{1}{n}\quad\textrm{and}\quad\overline{\delta}(A) = \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{\log N}\sum_{n\in A\cap [1,N]}\frac{1}{n}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Logarithmic densities: liminf/limsup of (1/log N) times the sum of 1/n over A ∩ [1,N].

nodes.name: Upper logarithmic density version of the density theorem
nodes.statement: A straightforward application of partial summation shows that $\overline{\delta}(A)\leq \overline{d}(A)$, and hence the analogue of Theorem~\ref{th-dens} with upper logarithmic density is an immediate corollary.
conclusions: $\overline{\delta}(A)\leq \overline{d}(A)$
the analogue of Theorem~\ref{th-dens} with upper logarithmic density is an immediate corollary
nodes.statement_short: Upper log density is at most upper density, so Theorem 2 also holds for positive upper logarithmic density.

nodes.name: Quantitative unit fraction theorem
nodes.statement: There is a constant $C>0$ such that the following holds. If $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ and \[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\geq C \frac{\log \log\log N}{\log\log N}\log N\] then there is an $S\subset A$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$.
conclusions: There is a constant $C>0$ such that the following holds.
there is an $S\subset A$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$
nodes.statement_short: If A ⊂ [1,N] has R(A) ≥ C (logloglog N / loglog N) log N then some S ⊂ A has sum of reciprocals 1.
nodes.label: th-quant

nodes.name: lambda(N): extremal reciprocal sum without unit-fraction solution
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda(N)$ be the maximum possible size of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$ if $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ has no subset $S$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$.
also_stated_at: Recall that $\lambda(N)$ is the maximum of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$ as $A$ ranges over those $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no subsets $S\subset A$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$.
nodes.statement_short: λ(N) is the largest reciprocal sum of a set in [1,N] with no subset whose reciprocals sum to 1.

nodes.name: Primes give lambda(N) >> log log N
nodes.statement: The primes show that\footnote{We use Vinogradov's notation $f\ll g$ to denote the existence of some absolute constant $C>0$ such that $\abs{f(n)}\leq C\abs{g(n)}$ for all sufficiently large $n$.} $\lambda(N) \gg \log\log N$.
conclusions: $\lambda(N) \gg \log\log N$
nodes.statement_short: Taking A to be the primes shows λ(N) ≫ log log N.

nodes.name: Current bounds for lambda(N)
nodes.statement: This is the best lower bound that we are aware of, so that our current state of knowledge is now \[(\log\log N)^2 \ll \lambda(N) \ll \frac{\log \log\log N}{\log\log N}\log N.\]
nodes.statement_short: Combining the bounds: (loglog N)^2 ≪ λ(N) ≪ (logloglog N/loglog N) log N.

nodes.name: lambda(N) <= (log N)^{o(1)}
nodes.statement: We suspect that the lower bound is closer to the truth, in that $\lambda(N)\leq (\log N)^{o(1)}$.
conclusions: $\lambda(N)\leq (\log N)^{o(1)}$

nodes.name: Croot's main theorem (smooth density statement)
nodes.statement: Roughly speaking, Croot proves that if $A\subset [2,N]$ has $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}> 6$ and all $n\in A$ are `$n^{1/4-o(1)}$-smooth' (i.e. if a prime power $q$ divides $n\in A$ then $q\leq n^{1/4-o(1)}$) then $A$ contains some $S$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$.
assumptions: all $n\in A$ are `$n^{1/4-o(1)}$-smooth' (i.e. if a prime power $q$ divides $n\in A$ then $q\leq n^{1/4-o(1)}$)
conclusions: $A$ contains some $S$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$
nodes.statement_short: A set of n^{1/4-o(1)}-smooth integers in [2,N] with reciprocal sum > 6 contains S with reciprocal sum 1.

nodes.name: R(A), reciprocal sum of A
nodes.statement: We introduce the convenient notation $R(A)=\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$ , which will be used throughout the rest of the paper.

nodes.name: Mertens' estimate for prime powers
nodes.statement: \sum_{q\leq X}\frac{1}{q}= \log\log X+c+O(1/\log X)\textrm{ for some constant }c,
assumptions: $q$ indicates the summation is restricted to prime powers
conclusions: \sum_{q\leq X}\frac{1}{q}= \log\log X+c+O(1/\log X)\textrm{ for some constant }c,
nodes.label: mertens1

nodes.name: Mertens' product estimate
nodes.statement: \prod_{p\leq X}\brac{1-\frac{1}{p}}^{-1}\asymp \log X,
assumptions: $p$ indicates the product is restricted to primes
conclusions: \prod_{p\leq X}\brac{1-\frac{1}{p}}^{-1}\asymp \log X,
nodes.label: mertens2

nodes.name: Main technical proposition
nodes.statement: Let $N$ be sufficiently large. Suppose $A\subset [N^{1-1/\log\log N},N]$ and $1\leq y\leq z\leq (\log N)^{1/500}$ are such that \begin{enumerate} \item $R(A)\geq 2/y+(\log N)^{-1/200}$, \item every $n\in A$ is divisible by some $d_1$ and $d_2$ where $y\leq d_1$ and $4d_1\leq d_2\leq z$, \item every prime power $q$ dividing some $n\in A$ satisfies $q\leq N^{1-6/\log\log N}$, and \item every $n\in A$ satisfies \[\tfrac{99}{100}\log\log N\leq \omega(n) \leq 2\log\log N.\] \end{enumerate} There is some $S\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d$ for some $d\in [y,z]$.
assumptions: every $n\in A$ is divisible by some $d_1$ and $d_2$ where $y\leq d_1$ and $4d_1\leq d_2\leq z$
every prime power $q$ dividing some $n\in A$ satisfies $q\leq N^{1-6/\log\log N}$
conclusions: There is some $S\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d$ for some $d\in [y,z]$.
nodes.statement_short: A large, smooth, regular set A in [N^{1-1/loglogN},N] whose elements all have two small divisors contains S with R(S)=1/d for some d in [y,z].
nodes.label: th-techmain

nodes.name: Why solve R(S)=1/d and the role of the small-divisor condition
nodes.statement: Before proceeding with the applications and proof of Proposition~\ref{th-techmain}, we make some further remarks about the reason we aim only to find a solution to $R(S)=1/d$ with $d$ small (instead of directly finding some $S$ with $R(S)=1$) and the utility of condition (2), that there exist some pair of small divisors. For simplicity we will only consider the case when $y=1$ and $z=4$, so that condition (2) becomes `every $n\in A$ is divisible by 4' and the conclusion becomes `there is some $S\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d$ for some $1\leq d\leq 4$'. Similar to Croot's method, we will would like to find solutions to $1=\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}$ using the circle method. Our formulation of the circle method (Proposition~\ref{prop-fourier} below) requires, amongst other assumptions, that \begin{enumerate} \item $R(A)\approx 2$ and \item a further technical hypothesis about the distribution of multiples of elements of $A$ in short intervals. \end{enumerate} (Roughly speaking, the first ensures that the `major arc' contribution is positive, and the second ensures that the `minor arc' contribution is small.) Since condition (1) of Proposition~\ref{th-techmain} says $R(A)>2$ we can arrange for $R(A)\approx 2$ by discarding some elements of $A$. Our conditions are not strong enough to force the second, technical, hypothesis, however. Following Croot, we aim to show that there is some subset $A'\subseteq A$ which satisfies this additional hypothesis via a combinatorial `pruning' technique. Unfortunately, to allow for the high `smoothness' threshold the additional hypothesis is quite restrictive, and therefore the pruning is severe. In particular, supposing we begin with $R(A)\approx 2$, our method shows that either $A$ itself satisfies the additional technical hypothesis, or else there is some pruned $B\subseteq A$ which does satisfy it -- but we have lost some of the mass of $A$, and can now only say that $R(B)\geq \frac{1}{3}R(A)\approx 2/3$. Since it is possible that $R(B)\approx 2/3$, whatever games we play we certainly cannot hope to find a solution to $R(S)=1$ with $S\subseteq B$! This means that we have to relax our initial goal, and instead be content with e.g. finding a solution to $R(S)=1/4$ (after pruning $B$ down a little further so that $R(B)\approx 2/4$ -- this is not strictly necessary in our simplified setup, but allowing for a small amount of further pruning eases some of the technical burdens in the general case). This introduces a further divisibility constraint however, since we can only hope to find a solution to $R(S)=1/4$ with $S\subseteq B$ if $4$ divides the lowest common multiple of $B$. This is where condition (2) becomes useful -- since every element of $A$ is divisible by $4$, certainly $4$ must divide the lowest common multiple of $B\subseteq A$. The universality of condition (2) is helpful here -- if there existed a subset of $A$, even a sparse one, that consisted of only odd numbers then it may be that our pruning procedure conspired so that $B$ is contained in this subset, and then we cannot find a solution to $R(S)=1/4$ with $S\subseteq B$. We hope that this sketch illustrates some of the issues involved and the reason for the particular form of Proposition~\ref{th-techmain}.
nodes.statement_short: Heuristic: pruning to satisfy the circle-method hypothesis loses mass, so one solves R(S)=1/d, which needs d | lcm, hence condition (2).

nodes.name: Corollary of the main technical proposition (R(S)=1)
nodes.statement: Suppose $N$ is sufficiently large and $A\subset [N^{1-1/\log\log N},N]$ is such that \begin{enumerate} \item $R(A)\geq (\log N)^{1/200}$, \item every $n\in A$ is divisible by some prime $p$ satisfying $5 \leq p \leq (\log N)^{1/500}$, \item every prime power $q$ dividing some $n\in A$ satisfies $q\leq N^{1-6/\log\log N}$, and \item every $n\in A$ satisfies \[\tfrac{99}{100}\log\log N\leq \omega(n) \leq 2\log\log N.\] \end{enumerate} There is some $S\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1$.
assumptions: every $n\in A$ is divisible by some prime $p$ satisfying $5 \leq p \leq (\log N)^{1/500}$
every prime power $q$ dividing some $n\in A$ satisfies $q\leq N^{1-6/\log\log N}$
conclusions: There is some $S\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Under conditions like Proposition 1 but with R(A) ≥ (log N)^{1/200} and a small prime divisor, some S ⊂ A has R(S)=1.
nodes.label: cor-techmain

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be maximal such that there are disjoint $S_1,\ldots,S_k\subset A$ where, for each $1\leq i\leq k$, there exists some $d_i\in [1,(\log N)^{1/500}]$ such that $R(S_i)=1/d_i$. Let $t(d)$ be the number of $S_i$ such that $d_i=d$. If there is any $d$ with $t(d)\geq d$ then we are done, taking $S$ to be the union of any $d$ disjoint $S_j$ with $R(S_j)=1/d$. Otherwise, \[\sum_i R(S_i)= \sum_{1\leq d\leq (\log N)^{1/500}} \frac{t(d)}{d}\leq (\log N)^{1/500},\] and hence if $A'=A\backslash (S_1\cup\cdots \cup S_k)$ then $R(A')\geq (\log N)^{1/500}$. We may now apply Proposition~\ref{th-techmain} with $y=1$ and $z=(\log N)^{1/500}$ -- note that condition (2) of Proposition~\ref{th-techmain} follows from condition (2) of Corollary~\ref{cor-techmain} with $d_1=1$ and $d_2=p\in [5,(\log N)^{1/500}]$ some suitable prime divisor. Thus there exists some $S'\subset A'$ such that $R(S')=1/d$ for some $d\in [1,(\log N)^{1/500}]$, contradicting the maximality of $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a maximal family of disjoint S_i with R(S_i)=1/d_i; either d of them share d, or the remainder still satisfies Proposition 1, contradicting maximality.

nodes.name: Maximal disjoint family
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be maximal such that there are disjoint $S_1,\ldots,S_k\subset A$ where, for each $1\leq i\leq k$, there exists some $d_i\in [1,(\log N)^{1/500}]$ such that $R(S_i)=1/d_i$. Let $t(d)$ be the number of $S_i$ such that $d_i=d$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a maximal family of disjoint S_i with R(S_i)=1/d_i and count t(d).

nodes.name: Case t(d) ≥ d
nodes.statement: If there is any $d$ with $t(d)\geq d$ then we are done, taking $S$ to be the union of any $d$ disjoint $S_j$ with $R(S_j)=1/d$.
nodes.statement_short: If some d has t(d) ≥ d, union d of them gives R(S)=1.

nodes.name: Case t(d) < d for all d
nodes.statement: Otherwise, \[\sum_i R(S_i)= \sum_{1\leq d\leq (\log N)^{1/500}} \frac{t(d)}{d}\leq (\log N)^{1/500},\] and hence if $A'=A\backslash (S_1\cup\cdots \cup S_k)$ then $R(A')\geq (\log N)^{1/500}$. We may now apply Proposition~\ref{th-techmain} with $y=1$ and $z=(\log N)^{1/500}$ -- note that condition (2) of Proposition~\ref{th-techmain} follows from condition (2) of Corollary~\ref{cor-techmain} with $d_1=1$ and $d_2=p\in [5,(\log N)^{1/500}]$ some suitable prime divisor. Thus there exists some $S'\subset A'$ such that $R(S')=1/d$ for some $d\in [1,(\log N)^{1/500}]$, contradicting the maximality of $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise the leftover A' is large and Proposition 1 gives another solution.

nodes.name: Leftover mass
nodes.statement: Otherwise, \[\sum_i R(S_i)= \sum_{1\leq d\leq (\log N)^{1/500}} \frac{t(d)}{d}\leq (\log N)^{1/500},\] and hence if $A'=A\backslash (S_1\cup\cdots \cup S_k)$ then $R(A')\geq (\log N)^{1/500}$.
nodes.statement_short: The S_i use little mass, so R(A') ≥ (log N)^{1/500}.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 1
nodes.statement: We may now apply Proposition~\ref{th-techmain} with $y=1$ and $z=(\log N)^{1/500}$ -- note that condition (2) of Proposition~\ref{th-techmain} follows from condition (2) of Corollary~\ref{cor-techmain} with $d_1=1$ and $d_2=p\in [5,(\log N)^{1/500}]$ some suitable prime divisor.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 1 to A' with y=1, z=(log N)^{1/500}.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Thus there exists some $S'\subset A'$ such that $R(S')=1/d$ for some $d\in [1,(\log N)^{1/500}]$, contradicting the maximality of $k$.
nodes.statement_short: The new S' contradicts maximality of k.

nodes.name: Sieve bound for integers avoiding primes in [y,z]
nodes.statement: Let $N$ be sufficiently large and $z,y$ be two parameters such that $\log N \geq z>y\geq 3$. If $X$ is the set of all those integers not divisible by any prime in $p\in [y,z]$ then \[\abs{ X\cap [N,2N)}\ll \frac{\log y}{\log z}N.\]
assumptions: $z,y$ be two parameters such that $\log N \geq z>y\geq 3$
$X$ is the set of all those integers not divisible by any prime in $p\in [y,z]$
conclusions: \[\abs{ X\cap [N,2N)}\ll \frac{\log y}{\log z}N.\]
nodes.statement_short: Integers in [N,2N) with no prime factor in [y,z] number ≪ (log y/log z) N.
nodes.label: lem-sieve1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Any sieve will suffice here, even the Sieve of Eratosthenes; for example, the formulation of the sieve of Eratosthenes as given in \cite[Theorem 3.1]{MV} yields \[\abs{X\cap [N,2N)} = \prod_{y\leq p\leq z}\brac{1-\frac{1}{p}}N+ O(2^z).\] Mertens' estimate \eqref{mertens2} yields \[\prod_{y\leq p\leq z}\brac{1-\frac{1}{p}}\asymp \frac{\log y}{\log z},\] and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Sieve of Eratosthenes plus Mertens' product estimate.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Let $C\geq 2$ be an absolute constant to be chosen shortly, and for brevity let $\epsilon = \log\log\log N/\log\log N$, so that we may assume that $R(A)\geq C\epsilon \log N$. Since $\sum_{n\leq X}\frac{1}{n}\ll \log X$, if $A'=A\cap [N^\epsilon,N]$ we have (assuming $C$ is sufficiently large) $R(A')\geq \frac{C}{2}\epsilon\log N$. Let $X$ be those integers $n\in [1,N]$ not divisible by any prime $p\in [5,(\log N)^{1/1200}]$. Lemma~\ref{lem-sieve1} implies that, for any $x\geq \exp(\sqrt{\log N})$, \[\abs{X\cap[x,2x)}\ll \frac{x}{\log\log N}\] and hence, by partial summation, \[\sum_{\substack{n\in X\\ n\in [\exp(\sqrt{\log N}),N]}}\frac{1}{n}\ll \frac{\log N}{\log\log N}.\] Similarly, if $Y$ is the set of those $N\in [1,N]$ such that $\omega(n) <\frac{99}{100}\log\log N$ or $\omega(n)\geq \frac{101}{100}\log\log N$ then Tur\'{a}n's estimate (see, for example, \cite[Theorem 2.12]{MV}) \[\sum_{n\leq x}(\omega(n)-\log\log n)^2\ll x\log\log x\] implies that $\abs{Y\cap [x,2x)}\ll x/\log\log N$ for any $N\geq x\geq \exp(\sqrt{\log N})$, and so \[\sum_{\substack{n\in Y\\ n\in [\exp(\sqrt{\log N}),N]}}\frac{1}{n}\ll \frac{\log N}{\log\log N}.\] In particular, provided we take $C$ sufficiently large, we can assume that $R(A'\backslash (X\cup Y))\geq \frac{C}{4}\epsilon \log N$, say. Let $\delta=1-1/\log\log N$, and let $N_i=N^{\delta^i}$, and $A_i=(A'\backslash (X\cup Y))\cap [N_{i+1},N_i]$. Since $N_i\leq N^{e^{-i/\log\log N}}$ and $A'$ is supported on $n\geq N^\epsilon$, the set $A_i$ is empty for $i> \log(1/\epsilon)\log\log N$, and hence by the pigeonhole principle there is some $i$ such that \[R(A_i)\geq \frac{C}{8}\frac{\epsilon\log N}{(\log\log N)\log(1/\epsilon)}.\] By construction, $A_i\subset [N_{i+1},N_i]\subset [N_i^{1-1/\log\log N_i},N_i]$, and every $n\in A_i$ is divisible by some prime $p$ with $5\leq p\leq (\log N)^{1/1200}\leq (\log N_i)^{1/500}$. Furthermore, every $n\in A_i$ satisfies $\omega(n)\geq \frac{99}{100}\log\log N\geq \frac{99}{100}\log\log N_i$ and $\omega(n)\leq \frac{101}{99}\log\log N\leq 2\log\log N_i$. Finally, it remains to discard the contribution of those $n\in A_i$ divisible by some large prime power $q> N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}$. The contribution to $R(A_i)$ of all such $n$ is at most \begin{align*} \sum_{N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}< q\leq N_i}\sum_{\substack{n\leq N_i\\ q\mid n}}\frac{1}{n} &\ll \sum_{N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}< q\leq N_i}\frac{\log(N_i/q)}{q}\\ &\ll \frac{\log N_i}{\log\log N_i}\sum_{N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}<q\leq N_i}\frac{1}{q}\\ &\ll \frac{\log N}{(\log\log N)^2}, \end{align*} using Mertens' estimate \eqref{mertens1}. Provided we choose $C$ sufficiently large, this is $\leq R(A_i)/2$, and hence, if $A_i'\subset A_i$ is the set of those $n$ divisible only by prime powers $q\leq N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}$, then $R(A_i')\geq (\log N)^{1/200}$, say. All of the conditions of Corollary~\ref{cor-techmain} are now met, and hence there is some $S\subset A_i'\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Discard small elements, sieve-exceptional and abnormal-ω integers, pigeonhole into a short dyadic-type range, remove large prime power multiples, then apply Corollary 1.

nodes.name: Discard small elements
nodes.statement: Let $C\geq 2$ be an absolute constant to be chosen shortly, and for brevity let $\epsilon = \log\log\log N/\log\log N$, so that we may assume that $R(A)\geq C\epsilon \log N$. Since $\sum_{n\leq X}\frac{1}{n}\ll \log X$, if $A'=A\cap [N^\epsilon,N]$ we have (assuming $C$ is sufficiently large) $R(A')\geq \frac{C}{2}\epsilon\log N$.
nodes.statement_short: Set ε and restrict to A' = A ∩ [N^ε, N], keeping half the mass.

nodes.name: Remove sieve exceptions
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be those integers $n\in [1,N]$ not divisible by any prime $p\in [5,(\log N)^{1/1200}]$. Lemma~\ref{lem-sieve1} implies that, for any $x\geq \exp(\sqrt{\log N})$, \[\abs{X\cap[x,2x)}\ll \frac{x}{\log\log N}\] and hence, by partial summation, \[\sum_{\substack{n\in X\\ n\in [\exp(\sqrt{\log N}),N]}}\frac{1}{n}\ll \frac{\log N}{\log\log N}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 1 and partial summation bound the mass of X (no small prime factor).

nodes.name: Remove abnormal ω
nodes.statement: Similarly, if $Y$ is the set of those $N\in [1,N]$ such that $\omega(n) <\frac{99}{100}\log\log N$ or $\omega(n)\geq \frac{101}{100}\log\log N$ then Tur\'{a}n's estimate (see, for example, \cite[Theorem 2.12]{MV}) \[\sum_{n\leq x}(\omega(n)-\log\log n)^2\ll x\log\log x\] implies that $\abs{Y\cap [x,2x)}\ll x/\log\log N$ for any $N\geq x\geq \exp(\sqrt{\log N})$, and so \[\sum_{\substack{n\in Y\\ n\in [\exp(\sqrt{\log N}),N]}}\frac{1}{n}\ll \frac{\log N}{\log\log N}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Turán's estimate bounds the mass of Y (ω(n) far from log log N).

nodes.name: Mass after removal
nodes.statement: In particular, provided we take $C$ sufficiently large, we can assume that $R(A'\backslash (X\cup Y))\geq \frac{C}{4}\epsilon \log N$, say.
nodes.statement_short: A' minus X ∪ Y still has mass ≥ (C/4) ε log N.

nodes.name: Pigeonhole over ranges
nodes.statement: Let $\delta=1-1/\log\log N$, and let $N_i=N^{\delta^i}$, and $A_i=(A'\backslash (X\cup Y))\cap [N_{i+1},N_i]$. Since $N_i\leq N^{e^{-i/\log\log N}}$ and $A'$ is supported on $n\geq N^\epsilon$, the set $A_i$ is empty for $i> \log(1/\epsilon)\log\log N$, and hence by the pigeonhole principle there is some $i$ such that \[R(A_i)\geq \frac{C}{8}\frac{\epsilon\log N}{(\log\log N)\log(1/\epsilon)}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Split into ranges [N_{i+1},N_i] and pigeonhole one A_i with large R(A_i).

nodes.name: Check conditions for A_i
nodes.statement: By construction, $A_i\subset [N_{i+1},N_i]\subset [N_i^{1-1/\log\log N_i},N_i]$, and every $n\in A_i$ is divisible by some prime $p$ with $5\leq p\leq (\log N)^{1/1200}\leq (\log N_i)^{1/500}$. Furthermore, every $n\in A_i$ satisfies $\omega(n)\geq \frac{99}{100}\log\log N\geq \frac{99}{100}\log\log N_i$ and $\omega(n)\leq \frac{101}{99}\log\log N\leq 2\log\log N_i$.
nodes.statement_short: A_i satisfies the range, small prime and ω conditions of Corollary 1.

nodes.name: Remaining: large prime powers
nodes.statement: Finally, it remains to discard the contribution of those $n\in A_i$ divisible by some large prime power $q> N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}$.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to remove n divisible by large prime powers.

nodes.name: Bound large prime power contribution
nodes.statement: The contribution to $R(A_i)$ of all such $n$ is at most \begin{align*} \sum_{N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}< q\leq N_i}\sum_{\substack{n\leq N_i\\ q\mid n}}\frac{1}{n} &\ll \sum_{N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}< q\leq N_i}\frac{\log(N_i/q)}{q}\\ &\ll \frac{\log N_i}{\log\log N_i}\sum_{N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}<q\leq N_i}\frac{1}{q}\\ &\ll \frac{\log N}{(\log\log N)^2}, \end{align*} using Mertens' estimate \eqref{mertens1}.
nodes.statement_short: Mertens bounds this contribution by log N/(loglog N)^2.

nodes.name: Remaining mass
nodes.statement: Provided we choose $C$ sufficiently large, this is $\leq R(A_i)/2$, and hence, if $A_i'\subset A_i$ is the set of those $n$ divisible only by prime powers $q\leq N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}$, then $R(A_i')\geq (\log N)^{1/200}$, say.
nodes.statement_short: After removal R(A_i') ≥ (log N)^{1/200}.

nodes.name: Apply Corollary 1
nodes.statement: All of the conditions of Corollary~\ref{cor-techmain} are now met, and hence there is some $S\subset A_i'\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 1 gives S ⊂ A with R(S)=1.

nodes.name: Sieve bound for integers without two separated primes in [y,z]
nodes.statement: Let $N$ be sufficiently large and $z,y$ be two parameters such that $(\log N)^{1/2}\geq z>4y\geq 8$. If $Y\subset [1,N]$ is the set of all those integers divisible by at least two distinct primes $p_1,p_2\in [y,z]$ where $4p_1<p_2$ then \[\abs{ \{1,\ldots,N\}\backslash Y}\ll \brac{\frac{\log y}{\log z}}^{1/2}N.\]
assumptions: $z,y$ be two parameters such that $(\log N)^{1/2}\geq z>4y\geq 8$
$Y\subset [1,N]$ is the set of all those integers divisible by at least two distinct primes $p_1,p_2\in [y,z]$ where $4p_1<p_2$
conclusions: \[\abs{ \{1,\ldots,N\}\backslash Y}\ll \brac{\frac{\log y}{\log z}}^{1/2}N.\]
nodes.statement_short: Integers up to N lacking two primes p1,p2 in [y,z] with 4p1<p2 number ≪ (log y/log z)^{1/2} N.
nodes.label: sieve2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Let $w\in (4y,z)$ be some parameter to be chosen later. Lemma~\ref{lem-sieve1} implies that the number of $n\in \{1,\ldots,N\}$ not divisible by any prime $p\in [w,z]$ is $\ll \frac{\log w}{\log z}N$. Similarly, for any $p\in [w,z]$, the number of those $n\in [1,N]$ divisible by $p$ and no prime $q\in [y,p/4)$ is \[\ll \frac{\log y}{\log p}\frac{N}{p}.\] It follows that the number of $n\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\backslash Y$ is \[\ll \brac{\frac{\log w}{\log z}+ \log y\sum_{p\geq w}\frac{1}{p\log p}}N.\] By partial summation, $\sum_{p\geq w}\frac{1}{p\log p}\ll 1/\log w$, and hence \[\abs{ \{1,\ldots,N\}\backslash Y}\ll \brac{\frac{\log w}{\log z}+\frac{ \log y}{\log w}}N.\] Choosing $w=\exp\brac{\sqrt{(\log y)(\log z)}}$ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 1 on [w,z] and to each p∈[w,z] with no prime in [y,p/4), sum by partial summation, optimise w.

nodes.name: No prime in [w,z]
nodes.statement: Let $w\in (4y,z)$ be some parameter to be chosen later. Lemma~\ref{lem-sieve1} implies that the number of $n\in \{1,\ldots,N\}$ not divisible by any prime $p\in [w,z]$ is $\ll \frac{\log w}{\log z}N$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 1 bounds integers with no prime factor in [w,z].

nodes.name: Fixed large prime p
nodes.statement: Similarly, for any $p\in [w,z]$, the number of those $n\in [1,N]$ divisible by $p$ and no prime $q\in [y,p/4)$ is \[\ll \frac{\log y}{\log p}\frac{N}{p}.\]
nodes.statement_short: For each p in [w,z], bound multiples of p with no prime in [y,p/4).

nodes.name: Sum over p
nodes.statement: It follows that the number of $n\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\backslash Y$ is \[\ll \brac{\frac{\log w}{\log z}+ \log y\sum_{p\geq w}\frac{1}{p\log p}}N.\] By partial summation, $\sum_{p\geq w}\frac{1}{p\log p}\ll 1/\log w$, and hence \[\abs{ \{1,\ldots,N\}\backslash Y}\ll \brac{\frac{\log w}{\log z}+\frac{ \log y}{\log w}}N.\]
nodes.statement_short: Sum over p using partial summation.

nodes.name: Optimise w
nodes.statement: Choosing $w=\exp\brac{\sqrt{(\log y)(\log z)}}$ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Choose w = exp(sqrt(log y log z)).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Suppose $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ has upper density $\delta>0$. Let $y=C_1/\delta$ and $z=\delta^{-C_2\delta^{-2}}$, where $C_1,C_2$ are two absolute constants to be determined later. It suffices to show that there is some $d\in [y,z]$ and finite $S\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d$. Indeed, given such an $S$ we can remove it from $A$ and still have an infinite set of upper density $\delta$, so we can find another $S'\subset A\backslash S$ with $R(S')=1/d'$ for some $d'\in [y,z]$, and so on. After repeating this process at least $\lceil z-y\rceil^2$ times there must be some $d\in [y,z]$ with at least $d$ disjoint $S_1,\ldots,S_d\subset A$ with $R(S_i)=1/d$. Taking $S=S_1\cup\cdots \cup S_d$ yields $R(S)=1$ as required. By definition of the upper density, there exist arbitrarily large $N$ such that $\abs{A\cap [1,N]}\geq \frac{\delta}{2}N$. The number of $n\in [1,N]$ divisible by some prime power $q\geq N^{1-6/\log\log N}$ is \[\ll N \sum_{N^{1-6/\log\log N}<q\leq N}\frac{1}{q}\ll \frac{N}{\log\log N}\] by Mertens' estimate \eqref{mertens1}. Further, by Tur\'{a}n's estimate \[\sum_{n\leq N}(\omega(n)-\log\log N)^2 \ll N \log\log N,\] the number of $n\in [1,N]$ that do not satisfy \begin{equation} \tfrac{99}{100}\log\log N\leq \omega(n) \leq 2\log\log N \end{equation} is $\ll N/\log\log N$. Finally, provided we choose $C_2$ sufficiently large in the definition of $z$, Lemma~\ref{sieve2} ensures that the proportion of all $n\in \{1,\ldots,N\}$ not divisible by at least two distinct primes $p_1,p_2\in [y,z]$ with $4p_1<p_2$ is at most $\frac{\delta}{8}N$, say. In particular, provided $N$ is chosen sufficiently large (depending only on $\delta$), we may assume that $\abs{A_N}\geq \frac{\delta}{4}N$, where $A_N\subset A$ is the set of those $n\in A\cap [N^{1-1/\log\log N},N]$ which satisfy conditions (2)-(4) of Proposition~\ref{th-techmain}. Since $\abs{A_N}\geq \frac{\delta}{4}N$, \[R(A_N) \gg -\log(1-\delta/4)\gg \delta.\] In particular, since $y=C_1/\delta$ for some suitably large constant $C_1>0$, we have that $R(A_N)\geq 4/y$, say. All of the conditions of Proposition~\ref{th-techmain} are now satisfied (provided $N$ is chosen sufficiently large in terms of $\delta$), and hence there is some $S\subset A_N\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d$ for some $d\in [y,z]$, which suffices to prove Theorem~\ref{th-dens} as discussed above.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to finding R(S)=1/d with d in [y,z] repeatedly; for large N choose A_N satisfying conditions (2)-(4) via Mertens, Turán and Lemma 2, then apply Proposition 1.

nodes.name: Parameters y, z
nodes.statement: Suppose $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ has upper density $\delta>0$. Let $y=C_1/\delta$ and $z=\delta^{-C_2\delta^{-2}}$, where $C_1,C_2$ are two absolute constants to be determined later.
nodes.statement_short: Fix δ, y = C1/δ and z = δ^{-C2 δ^{-2}}.

nodes.name: Reduction to 1/d
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that there is some $d\in [y,z]$ and finite $S\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to find S with R(S)=1/d for some d in [y,z].

nodes.name: Justify reduction
nodes.statement: Indeed, given such an $S$ we can remove it from $A$ and still have an infinite set of upper density $\delta$, so we can find another $S'\subset A\backslash S$ with $R(S')=1/d'$ for some $d'\in [y,z]$, and so on. After repeating this process at least $\lceil z-y\rceil^2$ times there must be some $d\in [y,z]$ with at least $d$ disjoint $S_1,\ldots,S_d\subset A$ with $R(S_i)=1/d$. Taking $S=S_1\cup\cdots \cup S_d$ yields $R(S)=1$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat removal; by pigeonhole some d gets d disjoint solutions, whose union has R=1.

nodes.name: Choose N
nodes.statement: By definition of the upper density, there exist arbitrarily large $N$ such that $\abs{A\cap [1,N]}\geq \frac{\delta}{2}N$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose arbitrarily large N with |A ∩ [1,N]| ≥ δN/2.

nodes.name: Few large prime power multiples
nodes.statement: The number of $n\in [1,N]$ divisible by some prime power $q\geq N^{1-6/\log\log N}$ is \[\ll N \sum_{N^{1-6/\log\log N}<q\leq N}\frac{1}{q}\ll \frac{N}{\log\log N}\] by Mertens' estimate \eqref{mertens1}.
nodes.statement_short: Mertens: few n ≤ N have a large prime power divisor.

nodes.name: Few abnormal ω
nodes.statement: Further, by Tur\'{a}n's estimate \[\sum_{n\leq N}(\omega(n)-\log\log N)^2 \ll N \log\log N,\] the number of $n\in [1,N]$ that do not satisfy \begin{equation} \tfrac{99}{100}\log\log N\leq \omega(n) \leq 2\log\log N \end{equation} is $\ll N/\log\log N$.
nodes.statement_short: Turán: few n ≤ N have ω(n) outside the range (3).

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Finally, provided we choose $C_2$ sufficiently large in the definition of $z$, Lemma~\ref{sieve2} ensures that the proportion of all $n\in \{1,\ldots,N\}$ not divisible by at least two distinct primes $p_1,p_2\in [y,z]$ with $4p_1<p_2$ is at most $\frac{\delta}{8}N$, say.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2: few n lack two separated primes in [y,z].

nodes.name: Define A_N
nodes.statement: In particular, provided $N$ is chosen sufficiently large (depending only on $\delta$), we may assume that $\abs{A_N}\geq \frac{\delta}{4}N$, where $A_N\subset A$ is the set of those $n\in A\cap [N^{1-1/\log\log N},N]$ which satisfy conditions (2)-(4) of Proposition~\ref{th-techmain}.
nodes.statement_short: The set A_N of good elements still has size ≥ δN/4.

nodes.name: Lower bound R(A_N)
nodes.statement: Since $\abs{A_N}\geq \frac{\delta}{4}N$, \[R(A_N) \gg -\log(1-\delta/4)\gg \delta.\] In particular, since $y=C_1/\delta$ for some suitably large constant $C_1>0$, we have that $R(A_N)\geq 4/y$, say.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 1
nodes.statement: All of the conditions of Proposition~\ref{th-techmain} are now satisfied (provided $N$ is chosen sufficiently large in terms of $\delta$), and hence there is some $S\subset A_N\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d$ for some $d\in [y,z]$, which suffices to prove Theorem~\ref{th-dens} as discussed above.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 1 yields S with R(S)=1/d, d in [y,z].

nodes.name: Normal order range for omega(n)
nodes.statement: \tfrac{99}{100}\log\log N\leq \omega(n) \leq 2\log\log N
nodes.label: divs

nodes.name: A_q and Q_A
nodes.statement: For any finite $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ and prime power $q$ we define \[A_q = \{ n\in A : q\mid n\textrm{ and }(q,n/q)=1\}\] and let $\mathcal{Q}_A$ be the set of all prime powers $q$ such that $A_q$ is non-empty (i.e. those $p^r$ such that $p^r\| n$ for some $n\in A$).
nodes.statement_short: A_q: elements of A exactly divisible by the prime power q; Q_A: the prime powers q with A_q non-empty.

nodes.name: Fourier-analytic (circle method) criterion for R(S)=1/k
nodes.statement: There is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that the following holds. Suppose that $N\geq M\geq N^{3/4}$ and $k$ is an integer satisfying $1\leq k\leq cM$. Suppose further that $\eta\in(0,1)$ and $M/2\geq K\geq N^{3/4}$. Let $A\subset [M,N]$ be a set of integers such that \begin{enumerate} \item $R(A)\in [2/k-1/M,2/k)$, \item $k$ divides the lowest common multiple of $A$, \item if $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$ then $q\leq c\min\brac{\frac{M}{k},\frac{\eta MK^2}{N^2(\log N)^2}}$, and \item for any interval $I$ of length $K$, either \begin{enumerate} \item \[\# \{ n\in A : \textrm{no element of }I\textrm{ is divisible by }n\}\geq M/\log N,\] or \item if $\mathcal{D}_I$ is the set of $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$ such that \[\#\{ n\in A_q: \textrm{no element of }I\textrm{ is divisible by }n\}<\eta \frac{M}{q},\] there is some $x\in I$ divisible by all $q\in\mathcal{D}_I$. \end{enumerate} \end{enumerate} There is some $S\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/k$. (In fact, there are at least $2^{\Omega(\abs{A})}$ many such $S$.)
assumptions: $k$ is an integer satisfying $1\leq k\leq cM$
$k$ divides the lowest common multiple of $A$

for any interval $I$ of length $K$, either \begin{enumerate} \item \[\# \{ n\in A : \textrm{no element of }I\textrm{ is divisible by }n\}\geq M/\log N,\] or \item if $\mathcal{D}_I$ is the set of $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$ such that \[\#\{ n\in A_q: \textrm{no element of }I\textrm{ is divisible by }n\}<\eta \frac{M}{q},\] there is some $x\in I$ divisible by all $q\in\mathcal{D}_I$.
conclusions: There is some $S\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/k$.
(In fact, there are at least $2^{\Omega(\abs{A})}$ many such $S$.)
nodes.statement_short: If R(A) is just below 2/k, k | lcm(A), all prime powers are small, and multiples of A are well distributed in intervals of length K, then some S ⊂ A has R(S)=1/k.
nodes.label: prop-fourier

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: For brevity, let $X= c\min(\frac{M}{k},\eta MK^2/N^2(\log N)^2)$, where $c>0$ is some absolute constant to be chosen later, so that condition (3) becomes $q\leq X$ for all $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$. For any set of prime powers $\mathcal{P}$ we write $[\mathcal{P}]$ for the lowest common multiple of all $q\in\mathcal{P}$. Since $A$ is fixed, in this proof we just write $\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}_A$. Let $F(A)$ count the number of subsets $S\subset A$ such that $kR(S)$ is an integer. Since $R(S)\leq R(A)<2/k$ and $R(S)=0$ if and only if $S=\emptyset$, the number of $S\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/k$ is exactly $F(A)-1$. We first note that, for any integers $a,b$, we have by orthogonality \[1_{a/b\in \mathbb{Z}} = \frac{1}{b}\sum_{-b/2< h\leq b/2}e\brac{\frac{ha}{b}},\] where $e(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$. In particular, since for any $S\subset A$ the rational $kR(S)$ is of the form $km/[\mathcal{Q}]$ for some $m\in \mathbb{Z}$, \[F(A)= \frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{-[\mathcal{Q}]/2< h\leq [\mathcal{Q}]/2}\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n)).\] The most obvious contribution to $F(A)$ is from $h=0$, which contributes exactly $2^{\abs{A}}/[\mathcal{Q}]$. Furthermore, if $[\mathcal{Q}]$ is even, then $h=[\mathcal{Q}]/2$ contributes \[\frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(k[\mathcal{Q}]/2n))\] which is some real number $\geq 0$, since $e(k[\mathcal{Q}]/2n)\in \{-1,1\}$ for all $n$ dividing $[\mathcal{Q}]$ (and so certainly for all $n\in A$). Therefore, \begin{equation} F(A)\geq \frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}+\frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{h\in J}\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n)) \end{equation} where $J= (-[\mathcal{Q}]/2,[\mathcal{Q}]/2)\cap \mathbb{Z}\backslash \{0\}$. Our treatment of $h\in J$ depends on whether $h$ is close to an integer of the form $t[\mathcal{Q}]/k$. We define the `major arc' corresponding to $t\in\mathbb{Z}$ as \[\mathfrak{M}(t) = \{ h\in J : \abs{h-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k}\leq K/2k\}\] (note that since $[\mathcal{Q}] \geq \min(A)\geq K$ the major arcs $\mathfrak{M}(t)$ are disjoint for distinct $t\in\mathbb{Z}$) and define the minor arcs as $\mathfrak{m} = J\backslash \cup_{t\in \mathbb{Z}}\mathfrak{M}(t)$. Writing $h\in\mathfrak{M}(t)$ as $t[\mathcal{Q}]/k+r$, the contribution of $\mathfrak{M}(t)$ to the right-hand side of \eqref{fbound} is, using $1+e(\theta)=2e(\theta/2)\cos(\pi \theta)$, \[ \frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{\substack{r\in [-K/2k,K/2k]\\ r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k} }\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kr/n))=\frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{\substack{r\in [-K/2k,K/2k]\\ r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k} }\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)e\brac{ \frac{kr}{2}R(A)}.\] The total contribution from all major arcs is therefore \[\frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{r\in [-K/2k,K/2k]}\brac{\sum_{t}1_{r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k}}\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)e\brac{ \frac{kr}{2}R(A)}.\] (Note that since $k\mid [\mathcal{Q}]$ the first factor restricts $r$ to be an integer.) Since both $\cos(\pi kr/n)$ and $\sum_t 1_{r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k}$ are symmetric in $r$, this is equal to \[\frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{r\in [0,K/2k]}(2-1_{r=0})\brac{\sum_{t}1_{r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k}}\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)\cos(\pi kr R(A)).\] Since $n\geq M\geq K$ and $0\leq r\leq K/2k$ we have $kr/n\leq 1/2$ and so certainly $\cos(\pi kr/n)\geq 0$. Furthermore, we can write $kR(A)=2-\epsilon$ for some $0<\epsilon\leq k/M$ and hence (since $r$ is an integer) \[\cos(\pi kr R(A)) = \cos(-\pi r\epsilon)\geq 0\] for $0\leq r\leq K/2k$, and hence \[\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)\cos(\pi kr R(A))\geq 0\] for all $0\leq r\leq K/2k$. It follows that the contribution to the right-hand side of \eqref{fbound} from the union of all $\mathfrak{M}(t)$ is $\geq 0$. It therefore suffices to show that \begin{equation} \sum_{h\in\mathfrak{m}}\prod_{n\in A}\abs{\cos(\pi kh/n)}\leq 1/4, \end{equation} say. Indeed, this implies that $F(A)\geq 2^{\abs{A}-1}/[\mathcal{Q}]$. Since all prime powers $q\in\mathcal{Q}$ satisfy $q\leq X$ we have the bound \[ [\mathcal{Q}]\leq X^{\pi(X)}\leq e^{O(X)}\leq 2^{\abs{A}/2},\] say, using Chebyshev's estimate that $\pi(X)\ll X/\log X$, the trivial estimate $\abs{A}\geq MR(A)\geq M/k$, and the fact that $X\leq cM/k$ (assuming $c$ sufficiently small). It follows that $F(A)\geq 2^{\abs{A}/2-1}>1$ as required. For any $h\geq 0$, let $\mathcal{D}_h=\mathcal{D}_{I_h}$ as defined in the theorem statement, where $I_h$ is the interval of length $K$ centred at $kh$. That is, $\mathcal{D}_h$ is the set of those $q\in \mathcal{Q}$ such that \[\#\{ n\in A_q:\abs{h_n}> K/2 \}< \eta \frac{M}{q},\] where $kh\equiv h_n \pmod{n}$ with $\abs{h_n}\leq n/2$. We introduce the convenient notation $C(B;h) = \prod_{n\in B}\abs{\cos(\pi kh/n)}$. Let $\mathfrak{m}_1$ be those $h\in\mathfrak{m}$ such that (4a) holds for $I_h$, and $\mathfrak{m}_2=\mathfrak{m}\backslash\mathfrak{m}_1$. We first address those $h\in\mathfrak{m}_1$. Note that if $x\in [0,1/2]$ then \[\cos(\pi x) \leq 1-x^2\leq e^{-x^2}.\] It follows that if $kh\equiv h_n \pmod{n}$, where $\abs{h_n}\leq n/2$, then \[\abs{\cos(\pi kh/n)}\leq e^{-\frac{h_n^2}{n^2}}.\] Further, if $h\in\mathfrak{m}_1$, then $\abs{h_n}\geq K/2$ for at least $M/\log N$ many $n\in A$, and hence \[C(A;h)\leq \exp\brac{-\sum_{n\in A}\frac{h_n^2}{n^2}}\leq \exp\brac{-\frac{K^2M}{4N^2\log N}}.\] Therefore \[\sum_{h\in\mathfrak{m}_1}C(A;h)\leq [\mathcal{Q}]\exp\brac{-\frac{K^2M}{4N^2\log N}}\leq e^{O(X)}\exp\brac{-\frac{K^2M}{4N^2\log N}}.\] Provided $X\leq c K^2M/N^2\log N$ for some sufficiently small constant $c>0$, this is $\leq 1/8$, and hence to show \eqref{tobound} it suffices to show \begin{equation} \sum_{h\in\mathfrak{m}_2}\prod_{n\in A}\abs{\cos(\pi kh/n)}\leq 1/8, \end{equation} We will show that, for any $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$, \begin{equation} C(A;h)\leq N^{-4\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash\mathcal{D}_h}}. \end{equation} (Note that this is trivial when $\mathcal{D}_h=\mathcal{Q}$.) Before establishing \eqref{tobound2}, we show how it implies \eqref{tobound3}, and hence concludes the proof. By condition (4b) of the hypotheses, since $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$, $kh$ is distance at most $K/2\leq M/2$ from some multiple of $[\mathcal{D}_h]$. Therefore, for any $\mathcal{D}\subset \mathcal{Q}$, the number of $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$ with $\mathcal{D}_h=\mathcal{D}$ is at most $M$ times the number of multiples of $[\mathcal{D}]$ in $[1,k[\mathcal{Q}]]$, which is at most \[Mk\frac{[\mathcal{Q}]}{[\mathcal{D}]} \leq Mk\prod_{q\in\mathcal{Q}\backslash\mathcal{D}}q\leq kN^{\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}+1}.\] In particular, by \eqref{tobound2}, the contribution to the left-hand side of \eqref{tobound3} from all $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$ with $\mathcal{D}_h=\mathcal{D}$ is at most $kN^{1-3\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}}$. By definition of $\mathfrak{m}$, if $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$ then $kh$ is distance greater than $K/2$ from any multiple of $[\mathcal{Q}]$, and hence $\mathcal{D}_h\neq \mathcal{Q}$. Therefore (using the trivial estimate $\abs{\mathcal{Q}}\leq N$) \begin{align*} \sum_{h\in\mathfrak{m}_2}C(A;h) &\leq kN\sum_{\mathcal{D}\subsetneq \mathcal{Q}}N^{-3\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}}\\ &\leq \frac{k}{N}(1+1/N)^{\abs{\mathcal{Q}}}\\ &\ll k/N \end{align*} which is $\leq 1/8$ provided $c$ is sufficiently small, which proves \eqref{tobound3}. It remains to establish \eqref{tobound2}. Using the trivial estimate $\omega(n)\ll \log n$, for any $n\in A$ there are $O(\log N)$ many $q\in\mathcal{Q}$ such that $n\in A_q$. It follows that \[C(A;h)\leq \prod_{q\in \mathcal{Q}}C(A_q;h)^{\Omega(1/\log N)}.\] To establish \eqref{tobound2}, therefore, it suffices to show that for every $q\in\mathcal{Q}\backslash\mathcal{D}_h$ we have $C(A_q;h)\leq N^{-C\log N}$ for some suitably large absolute constant $C>0$. For any $q\in\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}_h$ there are, by definition of $\mathcal{D}_h$, at least $\eta M/q$ many $n\in A_q$ such that $\abs{h_n}>K/2$ and hence \[C(A_q;h)\leq\exp\brac{-\sum_{n\in A_q}\frac{h_n^2}{n^2}}\leq \exp\brac{-\frac{\eta MK^2}{4N^2q}}.\] It therefore is enough to have that, for every $q\in\mathcal{Q}$, \[\frac{\eta MK^2}{4N^2q}\geq C(\log N)^2.\] This follows from $q\leq X\leq c\eta MK^2/N^2(\log N)^2$, provided $c$ is small enough.
nodes.statement_short: Circle method: count S with kR(S) integral by orthogonality; major arcs contribute non-negatively, minor arcs are bounded via cosine products. The key step is C(A;h) ≤ N^{-4|Q∖D_h|} on m_2 using condition (4b).

nodes.name: Notation X, [P], Q
nodes.statement: For brevity, let $X= c\min(\frac{M}{k},\eta MK^2/N^2(\log N)^2)$, where $c>0$ is some absolute constant to be chosen later, so that condition (3) becomes $q\leq X$ for all $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$. For any set of prime powers $\mathcal{P}$ we write $[\mathcal{P}]$ for the lowest common multiple of all $q\in\mathcal{P}$. Since $A$ is fixed, in this proof we just write $\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}_A$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce X, the lcm notation [P] and Q = Q_A.

nodes.name: Counting function F(A)
nodes.statement: Let $F(A)$ count the number of subsets $S\subset A$ such that $kR(S)$ is an integer. Since $R(S)\leq R(A)<2/k$ and $R(S)=0$ if and only if $S=\emptyset$, the number of $S\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/k$ is exactly $F(A)-1$.
nodes.statement_short: F(A) counts S with kR(S) integral; solutions number F(A)-1.

nodes.name: Reduction to the minor arc bound (5)
nodes.statement: We first note that, for any integers $a,b$, we have by orthogonality \[1_{a/b\in \mathbb{Z}} = \frac{1}{b}\sum_{-b/2< h\leq b/2}e\brac{\frac{ha}{b}},\] where $e(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$. In particular, since for any $S\subset A$ the rational $kR(S)$ is of the form $km/[\mathcal{Q}]$ for some $m\in \mathbb{Z}$, \[F(A)= \frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{-[\mathcal{Q}]/2< h\leq [\mathcal{Q}]/2}\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n)).\] The most obvious contribution to $F(A)$ is from $h=0$, which contributes exactly $2^{\abs{A}}/[\mathcal{Q}]$. Furthermore, if $[\mathcal{Q}]$ is even, then $h=[\mathcal{Q}]/2$ contributes \[\frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(k[\mathcal{Q}]/2n))\] which is some real number $\geq 0$, since $e(k[\mathcal{Q}]/2n)\in \{-1,1\}$ for all $n$ dividing $[\mathcal{Q}]$ (and so certainly for all $n\in A$). Therefore, \begin{equation} F(A)\geq \frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}+\frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{h\in J}\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n)) \end{equation} where $J= (-[\mathcal{Q}]/2,[\mathcal{Q}]/2)\cap \mathbb{Z}\backslash \{0\}$. Our treatment of $h\in J$ depends on whether $h$ is close to an integer of the form $t[\mathcal{Q}]/k$. We define the `major arc' corresponding to $t\in\mathbb{Z}$ as \[\mathfrak{M}(t) = \{ h\in J : \abs{h-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k}\leq K/2k\}\] (note that since $[\mathcal{Q}] \geq \min(A)\geq K$ the major arcs $\mathfrak{M}(t)$ are disjoint for distinct $t\in\mathbb{Z}$) and define the minor arcs as $\mathfrak{m} = J\backslash \cup_{t\in \mathbb{Z}}\mathfrak{M}(t)$. Writing $h\in\mathfrak{M}(t)$ as $t[\mathcal{Q}]/k+r$, the contribution of $\mathfrak{M}(t)$ to the right-hand side of \eqref{fbound} is, using $1+e(\theta)=2e(\theta/2)\cos(\pi \theta)$, \[ \frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{\substack{r\in [-K/2k,K/2k]\\ r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k} }\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kr/n))=\frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{\substack{r\in [-K/2k,K/2k]\\ r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k} }\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)e\brac{ \frac{kr}{2}R(A)}.\] The total contribution from all major arcs is therefore \[\frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{r\in [-K/2k,K/2k]}\brac{\sum_{t}1_{r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k}}\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)e\brac{ \frac{kr}{2}R(A)}.\] (Note that since $k\mid [\mathcal{Q}]$ the first factor restricts $r$ to be an integer.) Since both $\cos(\pi kr/n)$ and $\sum_t 1_{r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k}$ are symmetric in $r$, this is equal to \[\frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{r\in [0,K/2k]}(2-1_{r=0})\brac{\sum_{t}1_{r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k}}\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)\cos(\pi kr R(A)).\] Since $n\geq M\geq K$ and $0\leq r\leq K/2k$ we have $kr/n\leq 1/2$ and so certainly $\cos(\pi kr/n)\geq 0$. Furthermore, we can write $kR(A)=2-\epsilon$ for some $0<\epsilon\leq k/M$ and hence (since $r$ is an integer) \[\cos(\pi kr R(A)) = \cos(-\pi r\epsilon)\geq 0\] for $0\leq r\leq K/2k$, and hence \[\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)\cos(\pi kr R(A))\geq 0\] for all $0\leq r\leq K/2k$. It follows that the contribution to the right-hand side of \eqref{fbound} from the union of all $\mathfrak{M}(t)$ is $\geq 0$. It therefore suffices to show that \begin{equation} \sum_{h\in\mathfrak{m}}\prod_{n\in A}\abs{\cos(\pi kh/n)}\leq 1/4, \end{equation} say. Indeed, this implies that $F(A)\geq 2^{\abs{A}-1}/[\mathcal{Q}]$. Since all prime powers $q\in\mathcal{Q}$ satisfy $q\leq X$ we have the bound \[ [\mathcal{Q}]\leq X^{\pi(X)}\leq e^{O(X)}\leq 2^{\abs{A}/2},\] say, using Chebyshev's estimate that $\pi(X)\ll X/\log X$, the trivial estimate $\abs{A}\geq MR(A)\geq M/k$, and the fact that $X\leq cM/k$ (assuming $c$ sufficiently small). It follows that $F(A)\geq 2^{\abs{A}/2-1}>1$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Fourier-expand F(A), show major arcs contribute ≥ 0, reduce to (5).

nodes.name: Orthogonality
nodes.statement: We first note that, for any integers $a,b$, we have by orthogonality \[1_{a/b\in \mathbb{Z}} = \frac{1}{b}\sum_{-b/2< h\leq b/2}e\brac{\frac{ha}{b}},\] where $e(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$. In particular, since for any $S\subset A$ the rational $kR(S)$ is of the form $km/[\mathcal{Q}]$ for some $m\in \mathbb{Z}$, \[F(A)= \frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{-[\mathcal{Q}]/2< h\leq [\mathcal{Q}]/2}\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n)).\]
nodes.statement_short: Write F(A) as an exponential sum via orthogonality.

nodes.name: Lower bound (4)
nodes.statement: The most obvious contribution to $F(A)$ is from $h=0$, which contributes exactly $2^{\abs{A}}/[\mathcal{Q}]$. Furthermore, if $[\mathcal{Q}]$ is even, then $h=[\mathcal{Q}]/2$ contributes \[\frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(k[\mathcal{Q}]/2n))\] which is some real number $\geq 0$, since $e(k[\mathcal{Q}]/2n)\in \{-1,1\}$ for all $n$ dividing $[\mathcal{Q}]$ (and so certainly for all $n\in A$). Therefore, \begin{equation} F(A)\geq \frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}+\frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{h\in J}\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n)) \end{equation} where $J= (-[\mathcal{Q}]/2,[\mathcal{Q}]/2)\cap \mathbb{Z}\backslash \{0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: h=0 and h=[Q]/2 give the lower bound (4).

nodes.name: Major and minor arcs
nodes.statement: Our treatment of $h\in J$ depends on whether $h$ is close to an integer of the form $t[\mathcal{Q}]/k$. We define the `major arc' corresponding to $t\in\mathbb{Z}$ as \[\mathfrak{M}(t) = \{ h\in J : \abs{h-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k}\leq K/2k\}\] (note that since $[\mathcal{Q}] \geq \min(A)\geq K$ the major arcs $\mathfrak{M}(t)$ are disjoint for distinct $t\in\mathbb{Z}$) and define the minor arcs as $\mathfrak{m} = J\backslash \cup_{t\in \mathbb{Z}}\mathfrak{M}(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define major arcs M(t) and minor arcs m.

nodes.name: Major arc contribution
nodes.statement: Writing $h\in\mathfrak{M}(t)$ as $t[\mathcal{Q}]/k+r$, the contribution of $\mathfrak{M}(t)$ to the right-hand side of \eqref{fbound} is, using $1+e(\theta)=2e(\theta/2)\cos(\pi \theta)$, \[ \frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{\substack{r\in [-K/2k,K/2k]\\ r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k} }\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kr/n))=\frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{\substack{r\in [-K/2k,K/2k]\\ r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k} }\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)e\brac{ \frac{kr}{2}R(A)}.\] The total contribution from all major arcs is therefore \[\frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{r\in [-K/2k,K/2k]}\brac{\sum_{t}1_{r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k}}\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)e\brac{ \frac{kr}{2}R(A)}.\] (Note that since $k\mid [\mathcal{Q}]$ the first factor restricts $r$ to be an integer.)
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite major arc contribution as cosine products.

nodes.name: Major arcs non-negative
nodes.statement: Since both $\cos(\pi kr/n)$ and $\sum_t 1_{r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k}$ are symmetric in $r$, this is equal to \[\frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{r\in [0,K/2k]}(2-1_{r=0})\brac{\sum_{t}1_{r\in J-t[\mathcal{Q}]/k}}\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)\cos(\pi kr R(A)).\] Since $n\geq M\geq K$ and $0\leq r\leq K/2k$ we have $kr/n\leq 1/2$ and so certainly $\cos(\pi kr/n)\geq 0$. Furthermore, we can write $kR(A)=2-\epsilon$ for some $0<\epsilon\leq k/M$ and hence (since $r$ is an integer) \[\cos(\pi kr R(A)) = \cos(-\pi r\epsilon)\geq 0\] for $0\leq r\leq K/2k$, and hence \[\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)\cos(\pi kr R(A))\geq 0\] for all $0\leq r\leq K/2k$. It follows that the contribution to the right-hand side of \eqref{fbound} from the union of all $\mathfrak{M}(t)$ is $\geq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry and positivity of cosines, major arcs contribute ≥ 0.

nodes.name: Reduce to (5)
nodes.statement: It therefore suffices to show that \begin{equation} \sum_{h\in\mathfrak{m}}\prod_{n\in A}\abs{\cos(\pi kh/n)}\leq 1/4, \end{equation} say.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to show the minor arc bound (5).

nodes.name: (5) implies F(A)>1
nodes.statement: Indeed, this implies that $F(A)\geq 2^{\abs{A}-1}/[\mathcal{Q}]$. Since all prime powers $q\in\mathcal{Q}$ satisfy $q\leq X$ we have the bound \[ [\mathcal{Q}]\leq X^{\pi(X)}\leq e^{O(X)}\leq 2^{\abs{A}/2},\] say, using Chebyshev's estimate that $\pi(X)\ll X/\log X$, the trivial estimate $\abs{A}\geq MR(A)\geq M/k$, and the fact that $X\leq cM/k$ (assuming $c$ sufficiently small). It follows that $F(A)\geq 2^{\abs{A}/2-1}>1$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Bound [Q] by Chebyshev to get F(A) > 1.

nodes.name: Define D_h
nodes.statement: For any $h\geq 0$, let $\mathcal{D}_h=\mathcal{D}_{I_h}$ as defined in the theorem statement, where $I_h$ is the interval of length $K$ centred at $kh$. That is, $\mathcal{D}_h$ is the set of those $q\in \mathcal{Q}$ such that \[\#\{ n\in A_q:\abs{h_n}> K/2 \}< \eta \frac{M}{q},\] where $kh\equiv h_n \pmod{n}$ with $\abs{h_n}\leq n/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Define D_h via the interval I_h centred at kh.

nodes.name: Split minor arcs
nodes.statement: We introduce the convenient notation $C(B;h) = \prod_{n\in B}\abs{\cos(\pi kh/n)}$. Let $\mathfrak{m}_1$ be those $h\in\mathfrak{m}$ such that (4a) holds for $I_h$, and $\mathfrak{m}_2=\mathfrak{m}\backslash\mathfrak{m}_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Define C(B;h) and split minor arcs into m_1, m_2 by (4a).

nodes.name: Bound on m_1
nodes.statement: We first address those $h\in\mathfrak{m}_1$. Note that if $x\in [0,1/2]$ then \[\cos(\pi x) \leq 1-x^2\leq e^{-x^2}.\] It follows that if $kh\equiv h_n \pmod{n}$, where $\abs{h_n}\leq n/2$, then \[\abs{\cos(\pi kh/n)}\leq e^{-\frac{h_n^2}{n^2}}.\] Further, if $h\in\mathfrak{m}_1$, then $\abs{h_n}\geq K/2$ for at least $M/\log N$ many $n\in A$, and hence \[C(A;h)\leq \exp\brac{-\sum_{n\in A}\frac{h_n^2}{n^2}}\leq \exp\brac{-\frac{K^2M}{4N^2\log N}}.\] Therefore \[\sum_{h\in\mathfrak{m}_1}C(A;h)\leq [\mathcal{Q}]\exp\brac{-\frac{K^2M}{4N^2\log N}}\leq e^{O(X)}\exp\brac{-\frac{K^2M}{4N^2\log N}}.\] Provided $X\leq c K^2M/N^2\log N$ for some sufficiently small constant $c>0$, this is $\leq 1/8$, and hence to show \eqref{tobound} it suffices to show \begin{equation} \sum_{h\in\mathfrak{m}_2}\prod_{n\in A}\abs{\cos(\pi kh/n)}\leq 1/8, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: On m_1 cosine products are tiny; reduce to (6) on m_2.

nodes.name: State (7)
nodes.statement: We will show that, for any $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$, \begin{equation} C(A;h)\leq N^{-4\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash\mathcal{D}_h}}. \end{equation} (Note that this is trivial when $\mathcal{D}_h=\mathcal{Q}$.) Before establishing \eqref{tobound2}, we show how it implies \eqref{tobound3}, and hence concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: State the key bound (7) and plan to deduce (6) from it.

nodes.name: Count h with given D_h
nodes.statement: By condition (4b) of the hypotheses, since $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$, $kh$ is distance at most $K/2\leq M/2$ from some multiple of $[\mathcal{D}_h]$. Therefore, for any $\mathcal{D}\subset \mathcal{Q}$, the number of $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$ with $\mathcal{D}_h=\mathcal{D}$ is at most $M$ times the number of multiples of $[\mathcal{D}]$ in $[1,k[\mathcal{Q}]]$, which is at most \[Mk\frac{[\mathcal{Q}]}{[\mathcal{D}]} \leq Mk\prod_{q\in\mathcal{Q}\backslash\mathcal{D}}q\leq kN^{\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}+1}.\] In particular, by \eqref{tobound2}, the contribution to the left-hand side of \eqref{tobound3} from all $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$ with $\mathcal{D}_h=\mathcal{D}$ is at most $kN^{1-3\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}}$.
nodes.statement_short: By (4b), few h in m_2 share a given D_h.

nodes.name: Sum over D
nodes.statement: By definition of $\mathfrak{m}$, if $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$ then $kh$ is distance greater than $K/2$ from any multiple of $[\mathcal{Q}]$, and hence $\mathcal{D}_h\neq \mathcal{Q}$. Therefore (using the trivial estimate $\abs{\mathcal{Q}}\leq N$) \begin{align*} \sum_{h\in\mathfrak{m}_2}C(A;h) &\leq kN\sum_{\mathcal{D}\subsetneq \mathcal{Q}}N^{-3\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}}\\ &\leq \frac{k}{N}(1+1/N)^{\abs{\mathcal{Q}}}\\ &\ll k/N \end{align*} which is $\leq 1/8$ provided $c$ is sufficiently small, which proves \eqref{tobound3}.
nodes.statement_short: Summing over proper D ⊊ Q gives (6).

nodes.name: Remaining: (7)
nodes.statement: It remains to establish \eqref{tobound2}.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to prove (7).

nodes.name: Split over prime powers
nodes.statement: Using the trivial estimate $\omega(n)\ll \log n$, for any $n\in A$ there are $O(\log N)$ many $q\in\mathcal{Q}$ such that $n\in A_q$. It follows that \[C(A;h)\leq \prod_{q\in \mathcal{Q}}C(A_q;h)^{\Omega(1/\log N)}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Bound C(A;h) by a product of C(A_q;h).

nodes.name: Reduce (7) to each q
nodes.statement: To establish \eqref{tobound2}, therefore, it suffices to show that for every $q\in\mathcal{Q}\backslash\mathcal{D}_h$ we have $C(A_q;h)\leq N^{-C\log N}$ for some suitably large absolute constant $C>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices: C(A_q;h) ≤ N^{-C log N} for q outside D_h.

nodes.name: Bound C(A_q;h)
nodes.statement: For any $q\in\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}_h$ there are, by definition of $\mathcal{D}_h$, at least $\eta M/q$ many $n\in A_q$ such that $\abs{h_n}>K/2$ and hence \[C(A_q;h)\leq\exp\brac{-\sum_{n\in A_q}\frac{h_n^2}{n^2}}\leq \exp\brac{-\frac{\eta MK^2}{4N^2q}}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Many n in A_q have |h_n| > K/2, giving an exponential bound.

nodes.name: Conclude (7)
nodes.statement: It therefore is enough to have that, for every $q\in\mathcal{Q}$, \[\frac{\eta MK^2}{4N^2q}\geq C(\log N)^2.\] This follows from $q\leq X\leq c\eta MK^2/N^2(\log N)^2$, provided $c$ is small enough.
nodes.statement_short: Condition (3) on q gives the needed bound.

nodes.name: Lower bound for F(A) (4)
nodes.statement: F(A)\geq \frac{2^{\abs{A}}}{[\mathcal{Q}]}+\frac{1}{[\mathcal{Q}]}\sum_{h\in J}\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n))
nodes.label: fbound

nodes.name: Minor arc bound (5)
nodes.statement: \sum_{h\in\mathfrak{m}}\prod_{n\in A}\abs{\cos(\pi kh/n)}\leq 1/4,
nodes.label: tobound

nodes.name: Bound on m_2 (6)
nodes.statement: \sum_{h\in\mathfrak{m}_2}\prod_{n\in A}\abs{\cos(\pi kh/n)}\leq 1/8,
nodes.label: tobound3

nodes.name: Key bound C(A;h) (7)
nodes.statement: C(A;h)\leq N^{-4\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash\mathcal{D}_h}}.
nodes.label: tobound2

nodes.name: Croot's Lemma 2: reciprocal sum of common prime power divisors
nodes.statement: If $0<\abs{n_1-n_2}\leq N$ then \[\sum_{q\mid (n_1,n_2)}\frac{1}{q}\ll \log\log\log N,\] where the summation is restricted to prime powers.
assumptions: the summation is restricted to prime powers
conclusions: \[\sum_{q\mid (n_1,n_2)}\frac{1}{q}\ll \log\log\log N,\]
nodes.statement_short: For distinct n1, n2 within N, the reciprocal sum of common prime power divisors is ≪ logloglog N.
nodes.label: lem-basic

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: If $q\mid (n_1,n_2)$ then $q$ divides $\abs{n_1-n_2}$, and hence in particular $q\leq N$. The contribution of all prime powers $p^r$ with $r\geq 2$ is $O(1)$, and hence it suffices to show that $\sum_{p\mid \abs{n_1-n_2}}\frac{1}{p}\ll \log\log\log N$. Any integer $\leq N$ is trivially divisible by $O(\log N)$ many primes. Clearly summing $1/p$ over $O(\log N)$ many primes is maximised summing over the smallest $O(\log N)$ primes. Since there are $\gg (\log N)^{3/2}$ many primes $\leq (\log N)^2$, we have \[\sum_{p\mid \abs{n_1-n_2}}\frac{1}{p}\ll \sum_{p\leq (\log N)^2}\frac{1}{p}\ll \log\log\log N\] by Mertens' estimate \eqref{mertens1}.
nodes.statement_short: Common divisors divide n1-n2; few primes divide it, worst case is the smallest primes, then Mertens.

nodes.name: q divides the difference
nodes.statement: If $q\mid (n_1,n_2)$ then $q$ divides $\abs{n_1-n_2}$, and hence in particular $q\leq N$.
nodes.statement_short: Common divisors divide |n1-n2| ≤ N.

nodes.name: Reduce to primes
nodes.statement: The contribution of all prime powers $p^r$ with $r\geq 2$ is $O(1)$, and hence it suffices to show that $\sum_{p\mid \abs{n_1-n_2}}\frac{1}{p}\ll \log\log\log N$. Any integer $\leq N$ is trivially divisible by $O(\log N)$ many primes. Clearly summing $1/p$ over $O(\log N)$ many primes is maximised summing over the smallest $O(\log N)$ primes.
nodes.statement_short: Higher powers contribute O(1); reduce to primes, worst case the smallest O(log N) primes.

nodes.name: Mertens bound
nodes.statement: Since there are $\gg (\log N)^{3/2}$ many primes $\leq (\log N)^2$, we have \[\sum_{p\mid \abs{n_1-n_2}}\frac{1}{p}\ll \sum_{p\leq (\log N)^2}\frac{1}{p}\ll \log\log\log N\] by Mertens' estimate \eqref{mertens1}.
nodes.statement_short: Sum over primes up to (log N)^2 by Mertens.

nodes.name: Lower bound for the reciprocal sum of Q_A
nodes.statement: Let $1/2>\epsilon>0$ and $N$ be sufficiently large, depending on $\epsilon$. If $A$ is a finite set of integers such that $R(A)\geq (\log N)^{-\epsilon/2}$ and $(1-\epsilon)\log\log N\leq \omega(n)\leq 2\log\log N$ for all $n\in A$ then \[\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q} \geq (1-2\epsilon)e^{-1}\log\log N.\]
assumptions: $A$ is a finite set of integers such that $R(A)\geq (\log N)^{-\epsilon/2}$
conclusions: \[\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q} \geq (1-2\epsilon)e^{-1}\log\log N.\]
nodes.statement_short: If R(A) is not too small and all n in A have ω(n) ≈ log log N, then the reciprocal sum over Q_A is ≥ (1-2ε)e^{-1} loglog N.
nodes.label: lem-rtop

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: Since, by definition, every integer $n\in A$ can be written uniquely as $q_1\cdots q_t$ for $q_i\in \mathcal{Q}_A$ for some $t\in I = [(1-\epsilon)\log\log N, 2\log\log N]$, we have that, since $t!\geq (t/e)^t$, \[R(A)\leq \sum_{t\in I}\frac{\brac{\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}}^t}{t!}\leq \sum_{t\in I}\brac{\frac{e}{t}\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}}^t.\] Since $(ex/t)^t$ is decreasing in $t$ for $x<t$, either $\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}\geq (1-\epsilon)\log\log N$ (and we are done), or the summand is decreasing in $t$, and hence we have \[(\log N)^{-\epsilon/2}\leq R(A)\leq 2\log\log N\brac{\frac{\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}}{(1-\epsilon)e^{-1}\log\log N}}^{(1-\epsilon)\log\log N}.\] The claimed bound follows, using the fact that $e^{-\frac{\epsilon}{2(1-\epsilon)}}\geq 1-\epsilon$ for $\epsilon\in (0,1/2)$, choosing $N$ large enough such that $(2\log\log N)^{2/\log\log N}\leq 1+\epsilon^2$, say.
nodes.statement_short: Expand R(A) as a sum over products of t prime powers, bound by (e/t Σ1/q)^t, and compare.

nodes.name: Multinomial bound
nodes.statement: Since, by definition, every integer $n\in A$ can be written uniquely as $q_1\cdots q_t$ for $q_i\in \mathcal{Q}_A$ for some $t\in I = [(1-\epsilon)\log\log N, 2\log\log N]$, we have that, since $t!\geq (t/e)^t$, \[R(A)\leq \sum_{t\in I}\frac{\brac{\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}}^t}{t!}\leq \sum_{t\in I}\brac{\frac{e}{t}\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}}^t.\]
nodes.statement_short: Bound R(A) by Σ_t (e/t Σ 1/q)^t.

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: Since $(ex/t)^t$ is decreasing in $t$ for $x<t$, either $\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}\geq (1-\epsilon)\log\log N$ (and we are done), or the summand is decreasing in $t$, and hence we have \[(\log N)^{-\epsilon/2}\leq R(A)\leq 2\log\log N\brac{\frac{\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}}{(1-\epsilon)e^{-1}\log\log N}}^{(1-\epsilon)\log\log N}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Either done, or the summand is decreasing and bounded by the smallest t.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The claimed bound follows, using the fact that $e^{-\frac{\epsilon}{2(1-\epsilon)}}\geq 1-\epsilon$ for $\epsilon\in (0,1/2)$, choosing $N$ large enough such that $(2\log\log N)^{2/\log\log N}\leq 1+\epsilon^2$, say.
nodes.statement_short: Rearrange using elementary inequalities.

nodes.name: R(A;q)
nodes.statement: For any finite $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ and prime power $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$ we define \[R(A;q) = \sum_{n\in A_q}\frac{q}{n}.\]

nodes.name: Finding a large divisor qd carrying much of R(A;q)
nodes.statement: There is a constant $c>0$ such that the following holds. Let $N\geq M\geq N^{1/2}$ be sufficiently large, and suppose that $1\leq k \leq c\log\log N$. Suppose that $A\subset [M,N]$ is a set of integers such that $\omega(n)\leq (\log N)^{1/k}$ for all $n\in A$. For all $q$ such that $R(A;q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/2}$ there exists $d$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $qd > M\exp(-(\log N)^{1-1/k})$, \item $\omega(d)\leq \tfrac{5}{\log k}\log\log N$, and \item \[\sum_{\substack{n\in A_q\\qd\mid n\\ (qd,n/qd)=1}}\frac{qd}{n}\gg \frac{R(A;q)}{(\log N)^{2/k}}.\] \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $A\subset [M,N]$ is a set of integers such that $\omega(n)\leq (\log N)^{1/k}$ for all $n\in A$
conclusions: there exists $d$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $qd > M\exp(-(\log N)^{1-1/k})$, \item $\omega(d)\leq \tfrac{5}{\log k}\log\log N$, and \item \[\sum_{\substack{n\in A_q\\qd\mid n\\ (qd,n/qd)=1}}\frac{qd}{n}\gg \frac{R(A;q)}{(\log N)^{2/k}}.\]
nodes.statement_short: For each q with R(A;q) not small there is d with qd large, ω(d) small, and the qd-part of A carrying ≫ R(A;q)/(log N)^{2/k}.
nodes.label: lem-usingq

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: Fix some $q$ with $R(A;q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/2}$. Let $D$ be the set of all $d$ such that if $p$ is a prime and $p^r \| d$ then \[p^r>y=\exp((\log N)^{1-2/k})\] and \[qd\in (M\exp(-(\log N)^{1-1/k}),N].\] We first claim that every $n\in A_q$ is divisible by some $qd$ with $d\in D$, such that $(qd,n/qd)=1$. This can be done greedily, just removing from $n/q$ all those prime power divisors $p^r\| n/q$ such that $p^r\leq y$, which removes at most \[y^{\omega(n)}\leq \exp((\log N)^{1-1/k}).\] We can therefore bound \[R(A;q) \leq \sum_{d\in D}\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\substack{n\in A_q\\ qd\mid n\\ (qd,n/qd)=1}}\frac{qd}{n}.\] We will control the contribution from those $d$ with $\omega(d)>\omega_0= \frac{5}{\log k}\log\log N$ with the trivial bound \[\sum_{\substack{n\in A_q\\ qd\mid n\\ (qd,n/qd)=1}}\frac{qd}{n} \leq \sum_{\substack{n\leq N\\ qd\mid n}}\frac{qd}{n}\ll \log N\] and Mertens' bound \eqref{mertens1}. Together these imply \begin{align*} \sum_{\substack{d\in D\\ \omega(d)>\omega_0}}\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\substack{n\in A_q\\ qd\mid n}}\frac{qd}{n} &\ll \log N\sum_{\substack{d\\ p^r\| d\implies y<p^r\leq N\\ \omega(d)\geq \omega_0}} \frac{1}{d}\\ &\ll k^{-\omega_0}\log N\sum_{\substack{d\\ p^r\| d\implies y<p^r\leq N}} \frac{k^{\omega(d)}}{d}\\ &\ll C_1^kk^{-\omega_0}\log N\prod_{y<p\leq N}(1+\frac{k}{p-1}) \\ &\leq k^{-\omega_0}\log N\brac{C_2\frac{\log N}{\log y}}^{k} \end{align*} for some absolute constants $C_1,C_2>0$. Recalling the definitions of $y$ and $\omega_0$, this is \[\leq C_2^kk^{-\omega_0}(\log N)^3\leq 1/\log N,\] say, for $N$ sufficiently large. It follows that \[\tfrac{1}{2}R(A;q)\leq \sum_{\substack{d\in D\\ \omega(d)\leq \omega_0}}\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\substack{n\in A_q\\ qd\mid n\\ (qd,n/qd)=1}}\frac{qd}{n} .\] The result follows since \[\sum_{d\in D}\frac{1}{d}\leq \sum_{\substack{d\\ p^r\| d\implies y<p^r\leq N}}\frac{1}{d} \ll \prod_{y<p\leq N}\brac{1-\frac{1}{p-1}}^{-1}\ll \frac{\log N}{\log y}\ll (\log N)^{2/k}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Greedily strip small prime powers to get qd | n, discard d with many prime factors via a Rankin-type bound, then average over d.

nodes.name: Set D
nodes.statement: Fix some $q$ with $R(A;q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/2}$. Let $D$ be the set of all $d$ such that if $p$ is a prime and $p^r \| d$ then \[p^r>y=\exp((\log N)^{1-2/k})\] and \[qd\in (M\exp(-(\log N)^{1-1/k}),N].\]
nodes.statement_short: Fix q and define the set D of admissible d.

nodes.name: Every n has such qd
nodes.statement: We first claim that every $n\in A_q$ is divisible by some $qd$ with $d\in D$, such that $(qd,n/qd)=1$. This can be done greedily, just removing from $n/q$ all those prime power divisors $p^r\| n/q$ such that $p^r\leq y$, which removes at most \[y^{\omega(n)}\leq \exp((\log N)^{1-1/k}).\]
nodes.statement_short: Greedy removal of small prime powers shows each n ∈ A_q has a divisor qd with d in D.

nodes.name: Decompose R(A;q)
nodes.statement: We can therefore bound \[R(A;q) \leq \sum_{d\in D}\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\substack{n\in A_q\\ qd\mid n\\ (qd,n/qd)=1}}\frac{qd}{n}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Bound R(A;q) by a sum over d in D.

nodes.name: Discard large ω(d)
nodes.statement: We will control the contribution from those $d$ with $\omega(d)>\omega_0= \frac{5}{\log k}\log\log N$ with the trivial bound \[\sum_{\substack{n\in A_q\\ qd\mid n\\ (qd,n/qd)=1}}\frac{qd}{n} \leq \sum_{\substack{n\leq N\\ qd\mid n}}\frac{qd}{n}\ll \log N\] and Mertens' bound \eqref{mertens1}. Together these imply \begin{align*} \sum_{\substack{d\in D\\ \omega(d)>\omega_0}}\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\substack{n\in A_q\\ qd\mid n}}\frac{qd}{n} &\ll \log N\sum_{\substack{d\\ p^r\| d\implies y<p^r\leq N\\ \omega(d)\geq \omega_0}} \frac{1}{d}\\ &\ll k^{-\omega_0}\log N\sum_{\substack{d\\ p^r\| d\implies y<p^r\leq N}} \frac{k^{\omega(d)}}{d}\\ &\ll C_1^kk^{-\omega_0}\log N\prod_{y<p\leq N}(1+\frac{k}{p-1}) \\ &\leq k^{-\omega_0}\log N\brac{C_2\frac{\log N}{\log y}}^{k} \end{align*} for some absolute constants $C_1,C_2>0$. Recalling the definitions of $y$ and $\omega_0$, this is \[\leq C_2^kk^{-\omega_0}(\log N)^3\leq 1/\log N,\] say, for $N$ sufficiently large.
nodes.statement_short: Rankin-type bound shows d with ω(d) > ω_0 contribute ≤ 1/log N.

nodes.name: Half the mass remains
nodes.statement: It follows that \[\tfrac{1}{2}R(A;q)\leq \sum_{\substack{d\in D\\ \omega(d)\leq \omega_0}}\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\substack{n\in A_q\\ qd\mid n\\ (qd,n/qd)=1}}\frac{qd}{n} .\]
nodes.statement_short: Half of R(A;q) comes from d with ω(d) ≤ ω_0.

nodes.name: Average over d
nodes.statement: The result follows since \[\sum_{d\in D}\frac{1}{d}\leq \sum_{\substack{d\\ p^r\| d\implies y<p^r\leq N}}\frac{1}{d} \ll \prod_{y<p\leq N}\brac{1-\frac{1}{p-1}}^{-1}\ll \frac{\log N}{\log y}\ll (\log N)^{2/k}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Since Σ 1/d ≪ (log N)^{2/k}, some d works.

nodes.name: Dichotomy proposition: pruning or interval divisibility
nodes.statement: Suppose $N$ is sufficiently large and $N\geq M\geq N^{1/2}$, and suppose that $A\subset [M,N]$ is a set of integers such that \[\tfrac{99}{100}\log\log N\leq \omega(n)\leq 2\log\log N\quad\textrm{for all}\quad n\in A,\] \[R(A)\geq (\log N)^{-1/101}\] and, for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_A$, \[R(A;q) \geq (\log N)^{-1/100}.\] Then either \begin{enumerate} \item there is some $B\subset A$ such that $R(B)\geq \tfrac{1}{3}R(A)$ and \[\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_{B}}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N,\] or \item for any interval of length $\leq MN^{-2/(\log \log N)}$, either \begin{enumerate} \item \[\# \{ n\in A : \textrm{no element of }I\textrm{ is divisible by }n\}\geq M/\log N,\] or \item if $\mathcal{D}_I$ is the set of $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$ such that \[\#\{ n\in A_q: \textrm{no element of }I\textrm{ is divisible by }n\}<\frac{M}{2q(\log N)^{1/100}},\] there is some $x\in I$ divisible by all $q\in\mathcal{D}_I$. \end{enumerate} \end{enumerate} If $\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$ then case (2) is guaranteed.
assumptions: $N$ is sufficiently large and $N\geq M\geq N^{1/2}$
conclusions: Then either \begin{enumerate} \item there is some $B\subset A$ such that $R(B)\geq \tfrac{1}{3}R(A)$ and \[\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_{B}}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N,\] or \item for any interval of length $\leq MN^{-2/(\log \log N)}$, either \begin{enumerate} \item \[\# \{ n\in A : \textrm{no element of }I\textrm{ is divisible by }n\}\geq M/\log N,\] or \item if $\mathcal{D}_I$ is the set of $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$ such that \[\#\{ n\in A_q: \textrm{no element of }I\textrm{ is divisible by }n\}<\frac{M}{2q(\log N)^{1/100}},\] there is some $x\in I$ divisible by all $q\in\mathcal{D}_I$.
case (2) is guaranteed

Then either \begin{enumerate} \item there is some $B\subset A$ such that $R(B)\geq \tfrac{1}{3}R(A)$ and \[\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_{B}}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N,\] or \item for any interval of length $\leq MN^{-2/(\log \log N)}$, either \begin{enumerate} \item \[\# \{ n\in A : \textrm{no element of }I\textrm{ is divisible by }n\}\geq M/\log N,\] or \item if $\mathcal{D}_I$ is the set of $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$ such that \[\#\{ n\in A_q: \textrm{no element of }I\textrm{ is divisible by }n\}<\frac{M}{2q(\log N)^{1/100}},\] there is some $x\in I$ divisible by all $q\in\mathcal{D}_I$.
case (2) is guaranteed

nodes.statement_short: Either a large subset B has small reciprocal sum over Q_B, or A satisfies the interval condition (4) of Proposition 2 for intervals of length M N^{-2/loglog N}; the latter holds if Q_A already has small reciprocal sum.
nodes.label: prop-tech

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement:
Let $I$ be any interval of length $\leq MN^{-2/(\log\log N)}$, and let $A_I$ be those $n\in A$ that divide some element of $I$. We may assume that $\abs{A ackslash A_I}< M/\log N$ (or else 2(a) holds), and we need to show that either there is some $x\in I$ divisible by all $q\in\mathcal{D}_I$, or the first case holds. Let $\mathcal{E}_I$ be the set of those $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$ such that $R(A_I;q)> 1/2(\log N)^{1/100}$. For every $q\in \mathcal{D}_I$, by definition, \[R(A_I; q) \geq R(A;q) -  rac{ rac{M}{2q(\log N)^{1/100}}} rac{q}{M}> rac{1}{2(\log N)^{1/100}},\] and hence in particular $\mathcal{D}_I\subset \mathcal{E}_I$. For any $q\in \mathcal{E}_I$ we may therefore apply Lemma~ef{lem-usingq} with $A$ replaced by $A_I$, and $k$ chosen such that $(\log N)^{1/k}=2\log\log N$. This produces some $d_q$ such that $qd_q>\abs{I}$ and $\omega(d_q)<	frac{1}{500}\log\log N$ (provided $N$ is sufficiently large), and \[\sum_{\substack{n\in A_I\ qd_q\mid n\ (qd_q,n/qd_q)=1}} rac{qd_q}{n}\gg  rac{1}{(\log N)^{1/100}(\log\log N)^2}.\] By definition of $A_I$, every $n\in A_I$ with $qd_q\mid n$ must divide some $x\in I$ -- in fact, they must all divide the same $x\in I$ (call this $x_q\in I$, say), since all such $x$ are in particular divisible by $qd_q>\abs{I}$, which can divide at most one element in $I$. Let \[A_I^{(q)}=\{ n/qd_q : n\in A_I	extrm{ with }qd_q\mid n	extrm{ and }(qd_q,n/qd_q)=1\}\] so that, assuming $N$ is sufficiently large, $R(A_I^{(q)})\geq (\log N)^{-1/99}$, say. We may therefore apply Lemma~ef{lem-rtop} with $\epsilon=2/99$ (note that since $\omega(n)\geq  rac{99}{100}\log\log N$ for $n\in A$ and $\omega(d_q)< rac{1}{500}\log\log N$, we must have $\omega(m)\geq  rac{97}{99}\log\log N$ for all $m\in A_I^{(q)}$). This implies that \[\sum_{r\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_I^{(q)}}} rac{1}{r}\geq  rac{95}{99}e^{-1}\log\log N.\] Trivially, $\mathcal{Q}_{A_I^{(q)}}\subset \mathcal{Q}_A$, and further by choice of $x_q$, all $r\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_I^{(q)}}$ divide $x_q$, and hence \[\sum_{\substack{r\mid x_q\ r\in \mathcal{Q}_A}} rac{1}{r}\geq  rac{95}{99}e^{-1}\log\log N\geq 0.35\log\log N.\] For any two $n_1
eq n_2\in I$, we have \[\sum_{q\mid (n_1,n_2)} rac{1}{q}\ll \log\log\log N\leq 0.01\log\log N\] for $N$ sufficiently large, by Lemma~ef{lem-basic}. It follows that if $\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A} rac{1}{q}\leq  rac{2}{3}\log\log N$ then there can be at most one such possible value for $x_q\in I$ as $q$ ranges over $\mathcal{E}_I$, and hence this common shared value of $x_q$ is an $x\in I$ divisible by all $q\in\mathcal{E}_I$, and hence certainly by all $q\in\mathcal{D}_I$, as required. Furthermore, since $\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A} rac{1}{q}\leq (1+o(1))\log\log N\leq 1.01\log\log N$, say, there must always be at most two distinct values of $x_q\in I$ as $q$ ranges over $\mathcal{E}_I$. If there is no $x\in I$ divisible by all $q\in\mathcal{D}_I$, there must be exactly two such values, say $w_1$ and $w_2$. Let $A^{(i)}=\{n\in A: n\mid w_i\}$ and $A^{(0)}=A ackslash (A^{(1)}\cup A^{(2)})$. Since every $q\in\mathcal{Q}_{A^{(1)}}$ divides $w_1$, \[\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_{A^{(1)}}} rac{1}{q}\leq \sum_{q\leq N} rac{1}{q}- \sum_{q\mid w_2} rac{1}{q}+ \sum_{q\mid (w_1,w_2)} rac{1}{q}\leq (1-	frac{95}{99}e^{-1}+o(1))\log\log N.\] For large enough $N$, the right-hand side is $\leq  rac{2}{3}\log\log N$, and similarly for $A^{(2)}$. Since $R(A^{(0)})+R(A^{(1)})+R(A^{(2)})\geq R(A)$, we are in the first case choosing $B=A^{(1)}$ or $B=A^{(2)}$, unless $R(A^{(0)})\geq R(A)/3$. In this latter case we will derive a contradiction. Let $A'\subset A^{(0)}$ be the set of those $n\in A_I\cap A^{(0)}$ such that if $n\in A_q$ then $q\in\mathcal{E}_I$. By definition of $\mathcal{E}_I$ and Mertens' estimate \eqref{mertens1}, \[R(A^{(0)} ackslash A')\leq  rac{\abs{A ackslash A_I}}{M}+\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A ackslash \mathcal{E}_I} rac{1}{q}R(A_I;q)\ll  rac{\log\log N}{(\log N)^{1/100}},\] and so in particular, since $R(A)\geq (\log N)^{-1/101}$, we have $R(A')\gg (\log N)^{-1/101}$. In particular, $\abs{A'}\gg M/(\log N)^{-1/101}$. Therefore there must exist some $x\in I$ (necessarily $x
eq w_1$ and $x
eq w_2$ since $A'\subset A^{(0)}$) such that, if $A''=\{ n\in A' : n\mid x\}$, then \[\abs{A''}\gg N^{2/\log\log N}(\log N)^{-1/101},\] and hence $\abs{A''}\geq N^{3/2\log\log N}$, say. However, if $n\in A''$ then both $n\mid x$ and $n\mid w_1w_2$ (since every $q$ with $n\in A_q$ is in $\mathcal{E}_I$ and so divides either $w_1$ or $w_2$), and hence $n$ divides \[(x,w_1w_2)\leq (x,w_1)(x,w_2)\leq \abs{x-w_1}\abs{x-w_2}\leq N^2.\] Therefore the size of $A''$ is at most the number of divisors of some fixed integer $m\leq N^2$, which is at most $N^{(1+o(1))2\log 2/\log\log N}$ (see \cite[Theorem 2.11]{MV}, for example), and hence we have a contradiction for large enough $N$, since $2\log 2< 3/2$.
nodes.statement_short: For a fixed interval I, Lemma 5 and Lemma 4 attach to each q ∈ E_I a point x_q ∈ I with many prime power divisors; Lemma 3 limits the number of distinct x_q to at most two. Two values w1, w2 give case (1) or a divisor-count contradiction.

nodes.name: Fix interval I
