nodes.statement: Let $I$ be any interval of length $\leq MN^{-2/(\log\log N)}$, and let $A_I$ be those $n\in A$ that divide some element of $I$. We may assume that $\abs{A\backslash A_I}< M/\log N$ (or else 2(a) holds), and we need to show that either there is some $x\in I$ divisible by all $q\in\mathcal{D}_I$, or the first case holds.
nodes.statement_short: Fix I, define A_I, and assume 2(a) fails.

nodes.name: D_I ⊂ E_I
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{E}_I$ be the set of those $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$ such that $R(A_I;q)> 1/2(\log N)^{1/100}$. For every $q\in \mathcal{D}_I$, by definition, \[R(A_I; q) \geq R(A;q) - \brac{\frac{M}{2q(\log N)^{1/100}}}\frac{q}{M}>\frac{1}{2(\log N)^{1/100}},\] and hence in particular $\mathcal{D}_I\subset \mathcal{E}_I$.
nodes.statement_short: Define E_I and show D_I ⊂ E_I.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5
nodes.statement: For any $q\in \mathcal{E}_I$ we may therefore apply Lemma~\ref{lem-usingq} with $A$ replaced by $A_I$, and $k$ chosen such that $(\log N)^{1/k}=2\log\log N$. This produces some $d_q$ such that $qd_q>\abs{I}$ and $\omega(d_q)<\tfrac{1}{500}\log\log N$ (provided $N$ is sufficiently large), and \[\sum_{\substack{n\in A_I\\ qd_q\mid n\\ (qd_q,n/qd_q)=1}}\frac{qd_q}{n}\gg \frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/100}(\log\log N)^2}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5 gives d_q with qd_q > |I| and much mass on qd_q.

nodes.name: Common point x_q
nodes.statement: By definition of $A_I$, every $n\in A_I$ with $qd_q\mid n$ must divide some $x\in I$ -- in fact, they must all divide the same $x\in I$ (call this $x_q\in I$, say), since all such $x$ are in particular divisible by $qd_q>\abs{I}$, which can divide at most one element in $I$.
nodes.statement_short: All these n divide the same x_q ∈ I.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 4
nodes.statement: Let \[A_I^{(q)}=\{ n/qd_q : n\in A_I\textrm{ with }qd_q\mid n\textrm{ and }(qd_q,n/qd_q)=1\}\] so that, assuming $N$ is sufficiently large, $R(A_I^{(q)})\geq (\log N)^{-1/99}$, say. We may therefore apply Lemma~\ref{lem-rtop} with $\epsilon=2/99$ (note that since $\omega(n)\geq \frac{99}{100}\log\log N$ for $n\in A$ and $\omega(d_q)<\frac{1}{500}\log\log N$, we must have $\omega(m)\geq \frac{97}{99}\log\log N$ for all $m\in A_I^{(q)}$). This implies that \[\sum_{r\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_I^{(q)}}}\frac{1}{r}\geq \frac{95}{99}e^{-1}\log\log N.\]
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4 applied to A_I^{(q)} gives a large reciprocal sum of prime powers.

nodes.name: Divisors of x_q
nodes.statement: Trivially, $\mathcal{Q}_{A_I^{(q)}}\subset \mathcal{Q}_A$, and further by choice of $x_q$, all $r\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_I^{(q)}}$ divide $x_q$, and hence \[\sum_{\substack{r\mid x_q\\ r\in \mathcal{Q}_A}}\frac{1}{r}\geq \frac{95}{99}e^{-1}\log\log N\geq 0.35\log\log N.\]
nodes.statement_short: Prime powers dividing x_q have reciprocal sum ≥ 0.35 loglog N.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3
nodes.statement: For any two $n_1\neq n_2\in I$, we have \[\sum_{q\mid (n_1,n_2)}\frac{1}{q}\ll \log\log\log N\leq 0.01\log\log N\] for $N$ sufficiently large, by Lemma~\ref{lem-basic}.
nodes.statement_short: Distinct points of I share little reciprocal prime power mass.

nodes.name: Small Σ1/q forces case (2)
nodes.statement: It follows that if $\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$ then there can be at most one such possible value for $x_q\in I$ as $q$ ranges over $\mathcal{E}_I$, and hence this common shared value of $x_q$ is an $x\in I$ divisible by all $q\in\mathcal{E}_I$, and hence certainly by all $q\in\mathcal{D}_I$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: If Σ_{Q_A} 1/q ≤ (2/3) loglog N, all x_q coincide, giving case (2).

nodes.name: At most two values
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}\leq (1+o(1))\log\log N\leq 1.01\log\log N$, say, there must always be at most two distinct values of $x_q\in I$ as $q$ ranges over $\mathcal{E}_I$. If there is no $x\in I$ divisible by all $q\in\mathcal{D}_I$, there must be exactly two such values, say $w_1$ and $w_2$.
nodes.statement_short: In general at most two values w1, w2 of x_q occur.

nodes.name: Split A by w_i
nodes.statement: Let $A^{(i)}=\{n\in A: n\mid w_i\}$ and $A^{(0)}=A\backslash (A^{(1)}\cup A^{(2)})$. Since every $q\in\mathcal{Q}_{A^{(1)}}$ divides $w_1$, \[\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_{A^{(1)}}}\frac{1}{q}\leq \sum_{q\leq N}\frac{1}{q}- \sum_{q\mid w_2}\frac{1}{q}+ \sum_{q\mid (w_1,w_2)}\frac{1}{q}\leq (1-\tfrac{95}{99}e^{-1}+o(1))\log\log N.\]
nodes.statement_short: Split A by divisibility of w1, w2 and bound Σ_{Q_{A^{(1)}}} 1/q.

nodes.name: Case (1) or contradiction
nodes.statement: For large enough $N$, the right-hand side is $\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$, and similarly for $A^{(2)}$. Since $R(A^{(0)})+R(A^{(1)})+R(A^{(2)})\geq R(A)$, we are in the first case choosing $B=A^{(1)}$ or $B=A^{(2)}$, unless $R(A^{(0)})\geq R(A)/3$. In this latter case we will derive a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Either B = A^{(1)} or A^{(2)} gives case (1), or R(A^{(0)}) ≥ R(A)/3.

nodes.name: Large A'
nodes.statement: Let $A'\subset A^{(0)}$ be the set of those $n\in A_I\cap A^{(0)}$ such that if $n\in A_q$ then $q\in\mathcal{E}_I$. By definition of $\mathcal{E}_I$ and Mertens' estimate \eqref{mertens1}, \[R(A^{(0)}\backslash A')\leq \frac{\abs{A\backslash A_I}}{M}+\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A\backslash \mathcal{E}_I}\frac{1}{q}R(A_I;q)\ll \frac{\log\log N}{(\log N)^{1/100}},\] and so in particular, since $R(A)\geq (\log N)^{-1/101}$, we have $R(A')\gg (\log N)^{-1/101}$.
nodes.statement_short: Mertens shows A' retains mass ≫ (log N)^{-1/101}.

nodes.name: Large A''
nodes.statement: In particular, $\abs{A'}\gg M/(\log N)^{-1/101}$. Therefore there must exist some $x\in I$ (necessarily $x\neq w_1$ and $x\neq w_2$ since $A'\subset A^{(0)}$) such that, if $A''=\{ n\in A' : n\mid x\}$, then \[\abs{A''}\gg N^{2/\log\log N}(\log N)^{-1/101},\] and hence $\abs{A''}\geq N^{3/2\log\log N}$, say.
nodes.statement_short: Pigeonhole gives x ∈ I with many divisors A'' from A'.

nodes.name: Divisor bound contradiction
nodes.statement: However, if $n\in A''$ then both $n\mid x$ and $n\mid w_1w_2$ (since every $q$ with $n\in A_q$ is in $\mathcal{E}_I$ and so divides either $w_1$ or $w_2$), and hence $n$ divides \[(x,w_1w_2)\leq (x,w_1)(x,w_2)\leq \abs{x-w_1}\abs{x-w_2}\leq N^2.\] Therefore the size of $A''$ is at most the number of divisors of some fixed integer $m\leq N^2$, which is at most $N^{(1+o(1))2\log 2/\log\log N}$ (see \cite[Theorem 2.11]{MV}, for example), and hence we have a contradiction for large enough $N$, since $2\log 2< 3/2$.
nodes.statement_short: All of A'' divide a fixed m ≤ N^2, contradicting the divisor bound.

nodes.name: Pruning lemma: making R(B;q) large for all q
nodes.statement: Let $N$ be sufficiently large and $A\subset [1,N]$. There exists $B\subset A$ such that \[R(B)\geq R(A)-\frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/200}}\] and $R(B;q)\geq 2/(\log N)^{1/100}$ for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_B$.
conclusions: There exists $B\subset A$ such that \[R(B)\geq R(A)-\frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/200}}\] and $R(B;q)\geq 2/(\log N)^{1/100}$ for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_B$.
nodes.statement_short: One can remove little reciprocal mass from A so that every q in Q_B has R(B;q) ≥ 2/(log N)^{1/100}.
nodes.label: lem-pisqa

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement: We construct a sequence of decreasing sets $A=A_0\supsetneq A_1\supsetneq\cdots \supsetneq A_i$ as follows. Given some $A_i$, if there is a prime power $q_i\in\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$ such that \[R(A_i;q_i)< \frac{2}{(\log N)^{1/100}},\] then we let $A_{i+1}=A_i\backslash (A_i)_{q_i}$. If no such $q_i$ exists then we halt the construction. This process must obviously terminate in some finite time (since some non-empty amount of $A_i$ is being removed at each step). Suppose that it halts at $A_j=B$, say. The amount lost from $R(A)$ at step $i$ is \[\sum_{n\in (A_i)_{q_i}}\frac{1}{n}=\frac{1}{q_i}R(A_i;q_i)< \frac{2}{q_i(\log N)^{1/100}},\] and furthermore each $q\leq N$ can appear as at most one such $q_i$, since after removing $(A_i)_{q_i}$ anything left in $A_i$ cannot have $q_i$ as a coprime divisor. It follows that \[R(B)> R(A) -\frac{2}{(\log N)^{1/100}}\sum_{q\leq N}\frac{1}{q}\geq R(A)-\frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/200}},\] since $\sum_{q\leq N}\frac{1}{q}\ll \log\log N$.
nodes.statement_short: Greedy pruning: repeatedly delete (A_i)_q for a q with small R(A_i;q); each q is used once, so the loss is bounded by Mertens.

nodes.name: Greedy pruning construction
nodes.statement: We construct a sequence of decreasing sets $A=A_0\supsetneq A_1\supsetneq\cdots \supsetneq A_i$ as follows. Given some $A_i$, if there is a prime power $q_i\in\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$ such that \[R(A_i;q_i)< \frac{2}{(\log N)^{1/100}},\] then we let $A_{i+1}=A_i\backslash (A_i)_{q_i}$. If no such $q_i$ exists then we halt the construction. This process must obviously terminate in some finite time (since some non-empty amount of $A_i$ is being removed at each step).
nodes.statement_short: Iteratively remove (A_i)_{q_i} for q_i with small R(A_i;q_i); this terminates.

nodes.name: Loss per step
nodes.statement: Suppose that it halts at $A_j=B$, say. The amount lost from $R(A)$ at step $i$ is \[\sum_{n\in (A_i)_{q_i}}\frac{1}{n}=\frac{1}{q_i}R(A_i;q_i)< \frac{2}{q_i(\log N)^{1/100}},\] and furthermore each $q\leq N$ can appear as at most one such $q_i$, since after removing $(A_i)_{q_i}$ anything left in $A_i$ cannot have $q_i$ as a coprime divisor.
nodes.statement_short: Each step loses < 2/(q_i (log N)^{1/100}) and each q is used at most once.

nodes.name: Total loss
nodes.statement: It follows that \[R(B)> R(A) -\frac{2}{(\log N)^{1/100}}\sum_{q\leq N}\frac{1}{q}\geq R(A)-\frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/200}},\] since $\sum_{q\leq N}\frac{1}{q}\ll \log\log N$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the losses over q ≤ N.

nodes.name: Pruning lemma: R(B) in a prescribed short interval
nodes.statement: Suppose that $N$ is sufficiently large and $N\geq M\geq N^{1/2}$. Let $\alpha > 2/(\log N)^{1/200}$ and $A\subset [M,N]$ be a set of integers such that \[R(A) \geq \alpha+\frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/200}}\] and if $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$ then $q\leq M/(\log N)^{1/100}$. There is a subset $B\subset A$ such that $R(B)\in [\alpha-1/M,\alpha)$ and, for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_B$, \[R(B;q)\geq \frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/100}}.\]
assumptions: $N$ is sufficiently large and $N\geq M\geq N^{1/2}$
$A\subset [M,N]$ be a set of integers such that \[R(A) \geq \alpha+\frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/200}}\]
conclusions: There is a subset $B\subset A$ such that $R(B)\in [\alpha-1/M,\alpha)$ and, for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_B$, \[R(B;q)\geq \frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/100}}.\]
nodes.statement_short: One can find B ⊂ A with R(B) ∈ [α-1/M, α) and R(B;q) ≥ (log N)^{-1/100} for all q in Q_B.
nodes.label: lem-pisq

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement: We first apply Lemma~\ref{lem-pisqa} to produce some $A'\subset A$ such that $R(A')\geq \alpha$ and $R(A';q) \geq 2/(\log N)^{1/100}$ for all $q\in\mathcal{Q}_{A'}$. We now argue that whenever $D$ is such that $R(D)\geq \alpha$ and $R(D;q) \geq (\log N)^{-1/100}$ for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_D$ there exists some $x\in D$ such that $R(D\backslash \{x\};q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/100}$ for all $q\in\mathcal{Q}_{D}$. Given this, the lemma immediately follows, since we can continue removing such elements from $A'$ one at time until $R(B)$ falls in the required interval. To see why the above fact holds, apply Lemma~\ref{lem-pisqa} to obtain some $B\subset D$ (such that $R(B)\geq (\log N)^{-1/200}$, and hence in particular $B$ is non-empty), and let $x$ be any element of $B$. If $x\not\in D_q$ then by definition $R(D\backslash\{x\};q)=R(D;q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/100}$. If $x\in D_q$ then $x\in B_q$, and so \[R(D\backslash\{x\};q)\geq R(B;q)-\frac{q}{x}\geq \frac{2}{(\log N)^{1/100}}-\frac{q}{M}\geq \frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/100}}\] as required.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 6, then remove elements one at a time; Lemma 6 again shows a removable element always exists.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 6
nodes.statement: We first apply Lemma~\ref{lem-pisqa} to produce some $A'\subset A$ such that $R(A')\geq \alpha$ and $R(A';q) \geq 2/(\log N)^{1/100}$ for all $q\in\mathcal{Q}_{A'}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6 gives A' with R(A') ≥ α and all R(A';q) large.

nodes.name: Removable element fact
nodes.statement: We now argue that whenever $D$ is such that $R(D)\geq \alpha$ and $R(D;q) \geq (\log N)^{-1/100}$ for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_D$ there exists some $x\in D$ such that $R(D\backslash \{x\};q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/100}$ for all $q\in\mathcal{Q}_{D}$. Given this, the lemma immediately follows, since we can continue removing such elements from $A'$ one at time until $R(B)$ falls in the required interval.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: some element can always be removed while keeping all R(D;q) large; this gives the lemma.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 6 to D
nodes.statement: To see why the above fact holds, apply Lemma~\ref{lem-pisqa} to obtain some $B\subset D$ (such that $R(B)\geq (\log N)^{-1/200}$, and hence in particular $B$ is non-empty), and let $x$ be any element of $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6 on D gives non-empty B; pick x in B.

nodes.name: Case x ∉ D_q
nodes.statement: If $x\not\in D_q$ then by definition $R(D\backslash\{x\};q)=R(D;q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/100}$.
nodes.statement_short: If x ∉ D_q, R(D;q) is unchanged.

nodes.name: Case x ∈ D_q
nodes.statement: If $x\in D_q$ then $x\in B_q$, and so \[R(D\backslash\{x\};q)\geq R(B;q)-\frac{q}{x}\geq \frac{2}{(\log N)^{1/100}}-\frac{q}{M}\geq \frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/100}}\] as required.
nodes.statement_short: If x ∈ D_q, then R drops by at most q/x ≤ q/M.

nodes.name: Proof idea for Proposition 1
nodes.statement: The idea is, after pruning the set into a suitable form by repeated applications of Lemma~\ref{lem-pisq}, an application of Proposition~\ref{prop-tech} ensures that the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop-fourier} are satisfied, which in turn delivers a solution to $R(S)=1/d$ for some suitable $d$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: prune with Lemma 7, use Proposition 3 to verify the hypotheses of Proposition 2, which gives R(S)=1/d.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Let $M=N^{1-1/\log\log N}$ and $d_i = \lceil y \rceil +i$. By repeated applications of Lemma~\ref{lem-pisq} we can find a sequence $A\supset A_0\supset A_1\supset\cdots \supset A_{t}$, where $d_t=\lceil z/4\rceil-1$, such that \[R(A_i)\in [2/d_i-1/M,2/d_i)\quad\textrm{ and }\quad R(A_i;q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/100}\textrm{ for all }q\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}.\] (Note that the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem-pisq} continue to hold since \[\frac{2}{d_i}-\frac{1}{M}\geq \frac{2}{d_{i}+1}+\frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/200}}\geq \frac{3}{(\log N)^{1/200}}\] for all $0\leq i\leq t$.) Let $0\leq j\leq t$ be minimal such that there is a multiple of $d_j$ in $A_j$. Such a $j$ exists by assumption, since every $n\in A$ is divisible by some $d\in[y,z/4)$. Suppose first that case (2) of Proposition~\ref{prop-tech} holds for $A_j$. The hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop-fourier} are now met with $k=d_j$, $\eta=1/2(\log N)^{1/100}$, and $K=MN^{-2/\log \log N}$. This yields some $S\subset A'\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d_j$ as required. Otherwise, Proposition~\ref{prop-tech} yields some $B\subset A_j$ such that \[R(B)\geq 2/3d_j-1/M\geq 1/2d_j+(\log N)^{-1/200}\] and where $\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_B}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$. Let $e_i = 4d_j+i$ and, once again, repeatedly apply Lemma~\ref{lem-pisq} to find a sequence $B\supset B_0\supset \cdots\supset B_r$, where $e_r=\lfloor z\rfloor$, such that \[R(B_i)\in [2/e_i-1/M,2/e_i)\quad\textrm{ and }\quad R(B_i;q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/100}\textrm{ for all }q\in \mathcal{Q}_{B_i}.\] By minimality of $j$, no $d\in [y,d_j)$ divides any element of $A_j$, and hence every $n\in A_j$ is divisible by some $e\in [4d_j,z]$. In particular, there must exist some $0\leq s\leq r$ such that $B_s$ contains a multiple of $e_s$. Furthermore, since $\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_{B_s}}\frac{1}{q}\leq \sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_B}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$ we must be in the second case of Proposition~\ref{prop-tech}. The hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop-fourier} are now met with $k=e_s$ and $\eta,K$ as above, and thus there is some $S\subset B_j\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/e_s$.
nodes.statement_short: Prune A by Lemma 7 into nested sets with R(A_i) ≈ 2/d_i; take j minimal with a multiple of d_j. Proposition 3 either gives Proposition 2's hypotheses directly or a pruned B with small Σ1/q, where repeating with e_i ≥ 4d_j forces case (2).

nodes.name: Nested pruning
nodes.statement: Let $M=N^{1-1/\log\log N}$ and $d_i = \lceil y \rceil +i$. By repeated applications of Lemma~\ref{lem-pisq} we can find a sequence $A\supset A_0\supset A_1\supset\cdots \supset A_{t}$, where $d_t=\lceil z/4\rceil-1$, such that \[R(A_i)\in [2/d_i-1/M,2/d_i)\quad\textrm{ and }\quad R(A_i;q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/100}\textrm{ for all }q\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}.\] (Note that the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem-pisq} continue to hold since \[\frac{2}{d_i}-\frac{1}{M}\geq \frac{2}{d_{i}+1}+\frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/200}}\geq \frac{3}{(\log N)^{1/200}}\] for all $0\leq i\leq t$.)
nodes.statement_short: Repeated Lemma 7 gives nested A_i with R(A_i) just below 2/d_i.

nodes.name: Minimal j
nodes.statement: Let $0\leq j\leq t$ be minimal such that there is a multiple of $d_j$ in $A_j$. Such a $j$ exists by assumption, since every $n\in A$ is divisible by some $d\in[y,z/4)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take j minimal so A_j contains a multiple of d_j.

nodes.name: Case (2) for A_j
nodes.statement: Suppose first that case (2) of Proposition~\ref{prop-tech} holds for $A_j$. The hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop-fourier} are now met with $k=d_j$, $\eta=1/2(\log N)^{1/100}$, and $K=MN^{-2/\log \log N}$. This yields some $S\subset A'\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d_j$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: If Proposition 3 case (2) holds, Proposition 2 applies with k=d_j.

nodes.name: Case (1) for A_j
nodes.statement: Otherwise, Proposition~\ref{prop-tech} yields some $B\subset A_j$ such that \[R(B)\geq 2/3d_j-1/M\geq 1/2d_j+(\log N)^{-1/200}\] and where $\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_B}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$. Let $e_i = 4d_j+i$ and, once again, repeatedly apply Lemma~\ref{lem-pisq} to find a sequence $B\supset B_0\supset \cdots\supset B_r$, where $e_r=\lfloor z\rfloor$, such that \[R(B_i)\in [2/e_i-1/M,2/e_i)\quad\textrm{ and }\quad R(B_i;q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/100}\textrm{ for all }q\in \mathcal{Q}_{B_i}.\] By minimality of $j$, no $d\in [y,d_j)$ divides any element of $A_j$, and hence every $n\in A_j$ is divisible by some $e\in [4d_j,z]$. In particular, there must exist some $0\leq s\leq r$ such that $B_s$ contains a multiple of $e_s$. Furthermore, since $\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_{B_s}}\frac{1}{q}\leq \sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_B}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$ we must be in the second case of Proposition~\ref{prop-tech}. The hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop-fourier} are now met with $k=e_s$ and $\eta,K$ as above, and thus there is some $S\subset B_j\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/e_s$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise prune B again with larger e_i, now in case (2), and apply Proposition 2.

nodes.name: Pruned set B
nodes.statement: Otherwise, Proposition~\ref{prop-tech} yields some $B\subset A_j$ such that \[R(B)\geq 2/3d_j-1/M\geq 1/2d_j+(\log N)^{-1/200}\] and where $\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_B}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 3 case (1) gives B with small Σ_{Q_B} 1/q.

nodes.name: Prune B
nodes.statement: Let $e_i = 4d_j+i$ and, once again, repeatedly apply Lemma~\ref{lem-pisq} to find a sequence $B\supset B_0\supset \cdots\supset B_r$, where $e_r=\lfloor z\rfloor$, such that \[R(B_i)\in [2/e_i-1/M,2/e_i)\quad\textrm{ and }\quad R(B_i;q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/100}\textrm{ for all }q\in \mathcal{Q}_{B_i}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Repeated Lemma 7 gives nested B_i with R(B_i) just below 2/e_i.

nodes.name: Choose s
nodes.statement: By minimality of $j$, no $d\in [y,d_j)$ divides any element of $A_j$, and hence every $n\in A_j$ is divisible by some $e\in [4d_j,z]$. In particular, there must exist some $0\leq s\leq r$ such that $B_s$ contains a multiple of $e_s$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality of j gives s with a multiple of e_s in B_s.

nodes.name: Case (2) guaranteed
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_{B_s}}\frac{1}{q}\leq \sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_B}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$ we must be in the second case of Proposition~\ref{prop-tech}.
nodes.statement_short: Small Σ1/q forces case (2) of Proposition 3.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 2
nodes.statement: The hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop-fourier} are now met with $k=e_s$ and $\eta,K$ as above, and thus there is some $S\subset B_j\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/e_s$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 2 with k=e_s gives R(S)=1/e_s.

nodes.name: Pomerance's lower bound for lambda(N)
nodes.statement: \[\lambda(N) \gg (\log\log N)^2.\]
also_stated_at: Pomerance has observed\footnote{To our knowledge, this observation has only appeared in the literature in the PhD thesis of Croot \cite{Crootphd}, who heard it from Pomerance via personal communication. We include a proof of this lower bound in an appendix for the convenience of the reader.} that taking all $n$ with a prime factor $p\gg n/\log n$ provides the lower bound $\lambda(N) \gg (\log\log N)^2$.
assumptions: $\lambda(N)$ is the maximum of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$ as $A$ ranges over those $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no subsets $S\subset A$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$
conclusions: \[\lambda(N) \gg (\log\log N)^2.\]

nodes.name: Proof of Pomerance's lower bound
nodes.statement: Let $C\geq 1$ be some absolute constant, to be chosen later, and let $A$ be the set of all those $n\in \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that, if $p$ is the largest prime divisor of $n$, then $p\log p> Cn$. Considering the contribution to the sum from all those $n$ with a fixed largest prime divisor separately, we see that \begin{align*} \sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n} &\geq \sum_{p\leq N/\log N}\frac{1}{p}\sum_{m\leq \log p/C}\frac{1}{m}\\ &\gg \sum_{p\leq N/\log N}\frac{\log\log p}{p}\\ &\gg (\log\log N)^2. \end{align*} It remains to prove that there are no distinct $n_1,\ldots,n_k\in A$ such that \[\frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k}=1.\] Suppose otherwise, and fix such $n_1,\ldots,n_k$. Let $p$ be the largest prime which divides any of $n_1,\ldots,n_k$, and suppose (without loss of generality) $n_1=pm_1<\cdots<n_l=pm_l$ are all those $n_i$ divisible by $p$. Then \[\frac{1}{p}\brac{\frac{1}{m_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{m_l}}=1-\frac{1}{n_{l+1}}-\cdots-\frac{1}{n_k},\] where the right-hand side is some fraction whose denominator is not divisible by $p$. Therefore $p$ must divide the numerator of $\frac{1}{m_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{m_l}$, and hence $p$ divides \[[m_1,\ldots,m_l]\brac{\frac{1}{m_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{m_l}},\] where $[m_1,\ldots,m_l]$ is the lowest common multiple. Chebyshev's estimate shows that $[1,\ldots,m]\leq e^{O(m)}$ for all large enough $m$, and hence \[p\leq [1,\ldots,m_l]\brac{1+\frac{1}{2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{m_l}}\ll (\log m_l) e^{O(m_l)}\leq e^{O(m_l)}.\] It follows that $\log p\leq O(m_l)$, and so $n_l=pm_l\gg p\log p$. By construction, however, $p$ is the largest prime divisor of $n_l$, and hence $p\log p>Cn_l$, which is a contradiction for a suitable choice of $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Take n whose largest prime p has p log p > Cn; a solution would force p to divide a harmonic-sum numerator, giving p log p ≪ n, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Construction and its reciprocal sum
nodes.statement: Let $C\geq 1$ be some absolute constant, to be chosen later, and let $A$ be the set of all those $n\in \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that, if $p$ is the largest prime divisor of $n$, then $p\log p> Cn$. Considering the contribution to the sum from all those $n$ with a fixed largest prime divisor separately, we see that \begin{align*} \sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n} &\geq \sum_{p\leq N/\log N}\frac{1}{p}\sum_{m\leq \log p/C}\frac{1}{m}\\ &\gg \sum_{p\leq N/\log N}\frac{\log\log p}{p}\\ &\gg (\log\log N)^2. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Define A by the largest prime condition and show R(A) ≫ (loglog N)^2.

nodes.name: Remaining: no solution
nodes.statement: It remains to prove that there are no distinct $n_1,\ldots,n_k\in A$ such that \[\frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k}=1.\]
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show A has no unit fraction solution.

nodes.name: Isolate largest prime
nodes.statement: Suppose otherwise, and fix such $n_1,\ldots,n_k$. Let $p$ be the largest prime which divides any of $n_1,\ldots,n_k$, and suppose (without loss of generality) $n_1=pm_1<\cdots<n_l=pm_l$ are all those $n_i$ divisible by $p$. Then \[\frac{1}{p}\brac{\frac{1}{m_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{m_l}}=1-\frac{1}{n_{l+1}}-\cdots-\frac{1}{n_k},\] where the right-hand side is some fraction whose denominator is not divisible by $p$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose a solution exists; isolate the terms divisible by the largest prime p.

nodes.name: p divides numerator
nodes.statement: Therefore $p$ must divide the numerator of $\frac{1}{m_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{m_l}$, and hence $p$ divides \[[m_1,\ldots,m_l]\brac{\frac{1}{m_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{m_l}},\] where $[m_1,\ldots,m_l]$ is the lowest common multiple.
nodes.statement_short: p divides lcm(m_i) times the harmonic sum.

nodes.name: Chebyshev bound
nodes.statement: Chebyshev's estimate shows that $[1,\ldots,m]\leq e^{O(m)}$ for all large enough $m$, and hence \[p\leq [1,\ldots,m_l]\brac{1+\frac{1}{2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{m_l}}\ll (\log m_l) e^{O(m_l)}\leq e^{O(m_l)}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Chebyshev bounds p ≤ e^{O(m_l)}.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: It follows that $\log p\leq O(m_l)$, and so $n_l=pm_l\gg p\log p$. By construction, however, $p$ is the largest prime divisor of $n_l$, and hence $p\log p>Cn_l$, which is a contradiction for a suitable choice of $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence p log p ≪ n_l, contradicting p log p > C n_l.
